## Load the candidate pairs

The pairs in [`candidate_pairs.json`][pairs] come from two public music catalogs,
Wikidata and MusicBrainz. Both release this data under CC0, which puts it in the public
domain. In each pair, `entity_a` is an album record from Wikidata and `entity_b` is a
release from MusicBrainz. Each entity has four fields: title, artist, year, and label.
[`DATA_LICENSE.md`][license-data] credits both sources.

Each pair also has `known_same_as`. It is true when a Wikidata editor linked the album to
the MusicBrainz release group that the release belongs to. Wikidata is a knowledge graph,
and that link is an entity alignment link. The 70 pairs marked true are called *known
matches* here. In the other 380, the Wikidata album links to a different MusicBrainz entry.
Nobody checked each pair by hand.

The text is left exactly as the catalogs publish it, with no cleanup: mixed casing and
alphabet systems, straight and curly apostrophes, and placeholders such as `[no label]`.
A missing value is `-`.

We send one request per pair, so the number of requests depends on the number of
candidate pairs, not the size of either catalog.

```python theme={null}
DATA = Path("candidate_pairs.json")
DATA_URL = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/main/"
    "cookbooks/entity_alignment/candidate_pairs.json"
)
if not DATA.exists():
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(DATA_URL, DATA)

PAIRS = json.loads(DATA.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
BY_ID = {pair["id"]: pair for pair in PAIRS}

print(f"{len(PAIRS)} candidate pairs. The first one, as the model will see it:")
print(json.dumps({k: PAIRS[0][k] for k in ("entity_a", "entity_b")}, indent=2))
```

```

    "artist": "Alessandra Samadello",
    "year": "2003",
    "label": "-"
  },
  "entity_b": {
    "title": "My Refuge",
    "artist": "Kent Henry",
    "year": "1989",
    "label": "Hosanna! Music"
  }
}
```

## Ask one Score question and three Noul questions per candidate pair

The decision is a `Score` question because a `Score` attaches a written description to
each outcome in `LEVELS`, including the uncertain middle one, and keeps the three
outcomes in order. A `Noul` question could reach the middle outcome only indirectly, by
thresholding its output. A `Choice` question would lose the order of the three outcomes.

Put both entities into one state, as `entity_a` and `entity_b`, so each question is about
the pair. All four questions go in one request.
Title, artist, and label each get a `Noul` question to indicate where the records
disagree.

We round the score to the nearest level in `route()`. Write the level
descriptions before looking at the scores; the cut points follow from rounding rather
than being fitted to this dataset.

The middle level's wording decides which pairs reach a curator instead of being merged or
left unlinked, so it names the cases that need one: a reissue, a compilation, a special or
live edition, or a title that could refer to either album.

The merge recommendation is called `assert sameAs`: a recommendation to record that the
two entities are the same thing. That label is all `route()` returns; applying it to a
graph is a separate step.

There is no `Noul` question for the year, but the year is in the state.
For a year check, compare the two years in code and allow for a missing `-`.

The label question needs a rule, because catalogs disagree about which company to name.
We count a shortened name or a regional branch as the same label (*Columbia Records* and
*Columbia*, *EMI* and *EMI Music Brasil*). An imprint is a brand name a record company
releases under. We count an imprint and its parent company as different labels (*RCA
Victor* and *BMG*), because sharing a parent company does not establish that two albums
are the same.

To use this on another kind of data, swap in your own pairs and rewrite `QUESTIONS` and
`LEVELS`. The only other code that knows about albums is `show()`, which prints a pair
and names its fields.

```python expandable theme={null}
LEVELS = [
    "They describe two different albums.",
    "They describe closely related albums that may or may not be the same one: "
    "a reissue, a compilation, a special or live edition, or a title that could "
    "plausibly refer to either.",
    "They describe one and the same album.",
]
OUTCOME = {0: "leave unlinked", 1: "curator queue", 2: "assert sameAs"}

QUESTIONS = {
    "link_state": Score(
        instructions="How do the two entity descriptions relate as albums?",
        criteria=LEVELS,
    ),
    "same_title": Noul(
        instructions="Do the two entities give the same album title? Differences in "
        "casing, punctuation, or writing system (a title and its romanisation) do not "
        "make two titles different.",
    ),
    "same_artist": Noul(
        instructions="Do the two entities credit the same artist? A name written in "
        "another script or word order, or a credit that adds collaborators to the same "
        "lead artist, is the same artist.",
    ),
    "same_label": Noul(
        instructions="Do the two entities name the same record label? A shortened name "
        "or a regional branch of a label is the same label; an imprint and its parent "
        "company are different labels. A label of '-' or '[no label]' is not recorded.",
    ),
}


@json_cache
def score(state_json: str, questions_json: str) -> dict:
    """One request about one candidate pair -> the score plus the three noul answers."""
    questions = json.loads(questions_json)
    response = client.system_one(
        state=json.loads(state_json),
        questions=questions,
        model=TYPESAFE_MODEL,
    )
    link = response.answers["link_state"]
    return {
        "score": link.score,
        "probabilities": link.probabilities,
        "confidence": link.confidence,
        "properties": {
            k: response.answers[k].noul for k in questions if k != "link_state"
        },
    }


def score_pair(pair: dict) -> dict:
    state = {"entity_a": pair["entity_a"], "entity_b": pair["entity_b"]}
    questions = {k: q.model_dump(mode="json", exclude_none=True) for k, q in QUESTIONS.items()}
    return score(json.dumps(state), json.dumps(questions))


def route(score_value: float) -> str:
    """The whole decision rule: the nearest level names the outcome."""
    return OUTCOME[min(int(score_value + 0.5), len(LEVELS) - 1)]


def show(pair_id: str) -> None:
    pair = BY_ID[pair_id]
    result = score_pair(pair)
    print(
        f"{pair_id}  score {result['score']:.2f}  confidence {result['confidence']:.2f}"
        f"  ->  {route(result['score'])}"
    )
    for side in ("entity_a", "entity_b"):
        e = pair[side]
        print(
            f"    {e['title'][:40]:<42}{e['artist'][:26]:<28}{e['year']:<6}"
            f"{e['label'][:22]}"
        )
    nouls = result["properties"]
    print(
        f"    title {nouls['same_title']:.2f}   artist {nouls['same_artist']:.2f}   "
        f"label {nouls['same_label']:.2f}"
    )
```

```python theme={null}
for pair_id in ("c115", "c133", "c190", "c159"):
    show(pair_id)
    print()
```

```
c115  score 1.76  confidence 0.64  ->  assert sameAs
    Lions                                     The Black Crowes            2001  V2 Records
    Lions                                     The Black Crowes            2001  V2 Records Japan
    title 0.99   artist 0.99   label 0.94

c133  score 0.14  confidence 0.80  ->  leave unlinked
    Freak of Nature                           Anastacia                   2001  Epic Records
    Freak of Nature                           Taylor Deupree              1996  Rancho Relaxo
    title 0.99   artist 0.01   label 0.01

c190  score 1.27  confidence 0.55  ->  curator queue
    Head Hunters                              Herbie Hancock              1973  Columbia Records
    Headhunters                               Herbie Hancock              2008  Columbia
    title 0.71   artist 0.99   label 0.96

c159  score 0.75  confidence 0.62  ->  curator queue
    McCartney III                             Paul McCartney              2020  Capitol Records
    McCartney III Imagined                    Paul McCartney              2021  Capitol Records
    title 0.02   artist 0.98   label 0.99
```

In `c115` both sides are the same album, with the same title and
artist. The label is *V2 Records* on one side and *V2 Records Japan* on the other. In
`c133` the two sides are different albums that share a title. The other two round to the
middle level for different reasons. In `c190` one side is a 2008 reissue of a 1973 album,
with the title spelled as one word. In `c159` one side is an album and the other is a
remix album made from it.

## Route every candidate pair

```python expandable theme={null}
# 450 candidate pairs, one request each; a live run takes about a minute.
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=MAX_WORKERS) as pool:
    scored = list(pool.map(score_pair, PAIRS))

scores = [result["score"] for result in scored]
by_outcome: dict[str, list[str]] = {name: [] for name in OUTCOME.values()}
for pair, s in zip(PAIRS, scores):
    by_outcome[route(s)].append(pair["id"])

SURFACE, INK, INK2, MUTED = "#fcfcfb", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781"
GRID, AXIS, BLUE, ORANGE = "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"

BINS, TOP = 20, len(LEVELS) - 1
counts = [0] * BINS
for s in scores:
    counts[min(int(s / TOP * BINS), BINS - 1)] += 1
centers = [(i + 0.5) / BINS * TOP for i in range(BINS)]
queued = [c if route(x) == "curator queue" else 0 for c, x in zip(counts, centers)]
settled = [c if route(x) != "curator queue" else 0 for c, x in zip(counts, centers)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6), facecolor=SURFACE)
ax.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
for side in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
for side in ("left", "bottom"):
    ax.spines[side].set_color(AXIS)
ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED, labelcolor=INK2, labelsize=9)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, linewidth=0.8)
ax.bar(
    centers, settled, width=TOP / BINS * 0.9, color=BLUE, label="settled automatically"
)
ax.bar(
    centers, queued, width=TOP / BINS * 0.9, color=ORANGE, label="sent to the curator"
)
for edge in (0.5, 1.5):
    ax.axvline(edge, color=INK2, linewidth=1, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2])
ax.set_xticklabels(["0\ndifferent", "0.5", "1\nrelated", "1.5", "2\nsame"])
ax.set_xlabel("score for the pair", color=INK2, fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("candidate pairs", color=INK2, fontsize=9)
n_queued = len(by_outcome["curator queue"])
ax.set_title(
    f"{len(PAIRS) - n_queued} of {len(PAIRS)} pairs settled automatically;"
    f" {n_queued} go to the curator",
    loc="left",
    color=INK,
    fontsize=11,
)
ax.legend(frameon=False, labelcolor=INK2, fontsize=9)
display(fig)
plt.close(fig)

for name in ("assert sameAs", "curator queue", "leave unlinked"):
    n = len(by_outcome[name])
    print(f"{name:<16}{n:>5}  ({n / len(PAIRS):>5.1%})")
```

```
assert sameAs      57  (12.7%)
curator queue      79  (17.6%)
leave unlinked    314  (69.8%)
```

![output](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/8UawRogf0VplN_sC/cookbooks/entity_alignment/entity_alignment.executed.1.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=8UawRogf0VplN_sC\&q=85\&s=31b73ad6d566582e04236cf3cfd8f902)

The cut points are the two scores where `route()` changes its answer: 0.5 and 1.5. Most
pairs were routed without the curator: 314 scored below 0.5 and 57 scored at least 1.5,
which left 79 for the curator.

On this set, 257 of the 450 scores are between 0.1 and 0.4. Two different albums can
share a title, and a label name is weak evidence on its own, so the model gives the
middle level some probability even when a pair looks different. Routing depends only on
which side of a cut point the score falls: a pair at 0.4 is left unlinked, the same as a
pair at 0.

The three Noul answers help a curator inspect a pair, but only the Score decides its
route. Here are two pairs from the curator queue:

| Pair (Wikidata / MusicBrainz title) | Score | Same title | Same artist | Same label |
| :- | -: | -: | -: | -: |
| `c190` *Head Hunters* / *Headhunters* | 1.27 | 0.71 | 0.99 | 0.96 |
| `c159` *McCartney III* / *McCartney III Imagined* | 0.75 | 0.02 | 0.98 | 0.99 |

In `c190` the artist and label agree and the title nearly does, and the 35 years between
the two releases point to a reissue. In `c159` everything agrees except the title, which
suggests a related album rather than the same one.

## Compare with the catalogs' own answer

Nothing above used `known_same_as`. We count it for each outcome to compare the routing
with what the catalogs recorded.

```python theme={null}
print(f"{'':<16}{'known match':>13}{'known non-match':>17}")
for name in ("assert sameAs", "curator queue", "leave unlinked"):
    known = sum(BY_ID[pair_id]["known_same_as"] for pair_id in by_outcome[name])
    print(f"{name:<16}{known:>13}{len(by_outcome[name]) - known:>17}")
```

```
                  known match  known non-match
assert sameAs              48                9
curator queue              19               60
leave unlinked              3              311
```

The "known non-match" column counts the pairs where `known_same_as` is false. Of the 57
merges, 48 are known matches. Of the 314 pairs left unlinked, 311 are known non-matches.
The curator queue has 19 known matches and 60 known non-matches. The `known_same_as`
flag is not a checked answer, so this agreement is not a verified accuracy figure.

Some of the disagreements are mistakes in the catalogs. We looked up two of them in
MusicBrainz. In `c088`, both titles read *Um Novo Coração*, but the artists are Jozyanne
and Maíra. MusicBrainz has a separate entry for Jozyanne's album, and the Wikidata item
links to Maíra's instead, so `known_same_as` is true for two different albums. The model
left the pair unlinked. In `c415`, both sides are *Tonight: In Person* by The Limeliters,
from 1961 on RCA Victor. MusicBrainz lists the album twice and Wikidata links to the other
entry, so `known_same_as` is false. The model merged the pair. Six of the nine merged known
non-matches have the same title, artist, and year once case, punctuation, and accents are
ignored.

The model gets some pairs wrong too. It left two other known matches unlinked,
including `c444`, where one side credits *Justin Lo* and the other *側田*, the same singer's
Chinese name. Its `same_artist` answer is 0.03, and the pair scored 0.44, just under the
lower cut point.

```python theme={null}
for pair_id in ("c088", "c415"):
    show(pair_id)
    print()
```

```
c088  score 0.43  confidence 0.35  ->  leave unlinked
    Um Novo Coração                           Jozyanne                    2001  MK Music
    Um novo coração                           Maíra                       2001  Paradoxx Music
    title 0.97   artist 0.01   label 0.01

c415  score 1.97  confidence 0.97  ->  assert sameAs
    Tonight: In Person                        The Limeliters              1961  RCA Victor
    Tonight, In Person                        The Limeliters              1961  RCA Victor
    title 0.86   artist 0.99   label 0.99
```

```python theme={null}
)
```

# Feeder-cam visit log
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/feeder_watch

Send frames from bird feeder camera footage to Jev with five questions, one of them a Box that finds the bird, then use plain code to turn the answers into a visit log per species.

A camera on a bird feeder, a front door, or a street records hours of footage. Jev can
help you analyse it.

Send Jev the frames of a video one at a time and ask questions about each frame. With
footage from a bird feeder camera, the answers become a visit log per species.

![A snowy bird feeder with a male cardinal and a downy woodpecker, each in its own
labeled box with a species probability. A status bar shows the time, the bird\_present
probability, and the visits open so far.](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/l_j5jNYNp6JTBESY/cookbooks/feeder_watch/feeder-watch-hero.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=l_j5jNYNp6JTBESY\&q=85\&s=b18b39e8df73dcaa8cf0f5d4c30e9b0a)

We send Jev one frame a second, with five questions about each frame per request:

* `bird_present`, a `Noul`: is there a bird?
* `how_many`, a `Choice` of none, one, or several
* `bird`, a `Box`: where is the most prominent bird?
* `species_left` and `species_right`, two `Choice` questions over a list of species: what
  are the leftmost and rightmost birds?

A [Box](/primitives/box) question is used to find where the bird is in the image. It
returns one box, so when two species share the feeder, a second request asks for a box
around each species by name. This cookbook boxes up to two species at a time. Plain code
turns the answers into visits.

On the 101-second video clip we used, Jev agreed with our hand labels on whether a bird
was there in all 101 frames, and named the correct species in 132 of 133 labeled bird
sightings.

> **Note** - Images and Box questions are experimental ("dreamer-ready"). Every request
> that carries an image or a Box question needs the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true`
> header. See [Images](/images) and [Box](/primitives/box).

## Setup

Requires Python 3.10 or later. Choose a package manager to install the dependencies:

> [tab] pip
>
> Create a virtual environment and add the dependencies:
>
> ```bash wrap theme={null}
> python3 -m venv .venv
> .venv/bin/pip install 'typesafe-sdk>=0.7.5,<0.8.0' pillow matplotlib ipython
> ```

> [tab] uv
>
> Initialize a project and add the dependencies:
>
> ```bash wrap theme={null}
> uv init --bare
> uv add 'typesafe-sdk>=0.7.5,<0.8.0' pillow matplotlib ipython
> ```

Set your TypeSafe API key:

```bash theme={null}
export TYPESAFE_API_KEY="your-api-key"
```

Create a new file named `feeder_watch.py`. As you work through this cookbook, copy each
Python code block into that file, in order. This command runs it whether you installed
with pip or uv:

```bash theme={null}
.venv/bin/python feeder_watch.py
```

A full run sends about 180 requests. Pillow draws the boxes and matplotlib lays out the
figures.

Every response is saved in `json_cache.json`, so a second run makes no requests.

Numbers below came from `jev-1.14.0` on 2026-10-15.

```python theme={null}
import json
import os
import statistics
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path
from time import perf_counter

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display
from PIL import Image as PILImage
from PIL import ImageDraw, ImageFont
from cooksafe import JsonCache
from typesafe_sdk import Box, Choice, Image, Noul, SystemOneResponse, TypeSafeClient

TYPESAFE_MODEL = "jev-1.14.0"  # Box questions need Jev 1.14
IMAGE_HEADERS = {"TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images": "true"}  # images and Box are opt-in

client = TypeSafeClient(
    api_key=os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY", "cache-only"),  # keyless runs replay the cache
    timeout=60.0,
)
json_cache = JsonCache(Path("json_cache.json"))  # every response, keyed by frame and questions
```

## Download the frames

The footage is ["Busy Bird Feeder"][usfws-clip], a 101-second clip filmed by Courtney
Celley of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and released into the public domain. For the
first minute, a male cardinal and a downy woodpecker share the feeder, so most frames hold
two birds of different species. After that, the male cardinal leaves and a female cardinal
feeds from behind the feeder, mostly out of sight.

We cut one frame a second at 1024 × 576 pixels, and labeled each frame by hand with the
species of every bird in full view. Twenty-two frames are marked `partial`, because the
female cardinal in them is cut off at the edge or mostly hidden behind the feeder.
The frames are in [`usfws_frames.zip`][frames-zip] and the labels are in
[`usfws_labels.json`][labels-json], both in typesafe-public-examples. The source and the
changes made are in
[`DATA_LICENSE.md`][data-license]. The code below downloads both, unzips the frames into
`usfws_frames/`, and skips anything that is already on disk.

[usfws-clip]: https://www.flickr.com/photos/usfwsmidwest/31524812531

[data-license]: https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/blob/main/cookbooks/feeder_watch/DATA_LICENSE.md

[frames-zip]: https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/blob/main/cookbooks/feeder_watch/usfws_frames.zip

[labels-json]: https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/blob/main/cookbooks/feeder_watch/usfws_labels.json

```python theme={null}
EXAMPLES = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/main/"
    "cookbooks/feeder_watch"
)
FRAMES = Path("usfws_frames")
LABELS = Path("usfws_labels.json")


def download(url: str, path: Path) -> Path:
    if not path.exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, path)
    return path


if not FRAMES.exists():
    with zipfile.ZipFile(download(f"{EXAMPLES}/usfws_frames.zip", Path("usfws_frames.zip"))) as zf:
        zf.extractall()  # the zip holds usfws_frames/u001.jpg to u101.jpg
NAMES = [f"u{second:03d}.jpg" for second in range(1, 102)]  # one frame per second
paths = [FRAMES / n for n in NAMES]
labels = json.loads(download(f"{EXAMPLES}/usfws_labels.json", LABELS).read_text())

birds_per_frame = [len(labels[n]["species"]) for n in NAMES]
print(f"{len(paths)} frames, {PILImage.open(paths[0]).size[0]} x {PILImage.open(paths[0]).size[1]}")
print(f"frames by birds in full view: {[birds_per_frame.count(k) for k in (0, 1, 2)]} (0, 1, 2)")
print("u010.jpg is labeled", labels["u010.jpg"])
```

```
101 frames, 1024 x 576
frames by birds in full view: [11, 27, 63] (0, 1, 2)
u010.jpg is labeled {'species': ['cardinal_male', 'downy_woodpecker'], 'partial': False}
```

## Write the questions

Each request sends one frame as the state, under the key `frame`, and asks five questions
about it. All five share the one request, so the image is sent once.

* The `bird_present` question is a `Noul`. Below 0.5, the frame counts as empty and the
  code ignores the other answers. A Box question always returns a box, even when there is
  nothing to find, so this answer is what tells the code whether to use the box.
* The `how_many` question is a `Choice` over `none`, `one`, and `several`. The code asks
  for a second box only when the answer is `several`.
* The `bird` question is a `Box` around the most prominent bird. Frames with one bird use
  this box.
* The `species_left` and `species_right` questions are the same `Choice`, over ten species
  plus `other`, asked about the leftmost and the rightmost bird. With one bird in the
  frame, both answers describe it. With two, each answer describes one bird.

Each species option describes what the bird looks like on a feeder camera, rather than what
a field guide says. For example, the grackle option says the bird can fill the frame so
that only its head shows.

```python expandable theme={null}
SPECIES = {
    "blue_jay": "A blue bird with a crest, a pale grey-white face and chest, a black necklace, "
    "and black bars on the blue wings and tail.",
    "cardinal_male": "A bright red bird with a pointed crest, a black mask, and an orange beak.",
    "cardinal_female": "A warm brown or buff bird with a pointed crest, reddish tinges on the "
    "wings, tail and crest, and an orange beak.",
    "grackle": "A common grackle: a glossy black bird with a pale yellow eye, a long heavy dark "
    "beak, and an iridescent blue, purple or bronze sheen on the head and body. On a close-up "
    "feeder camera it often fills the frame, so only the glossy dark head, pale eye and beak "
    "may be visible.",
    "starling": "A European starling: a chunky short-tailed dark bird with glossy plumage "
    "speckled with pale spots, a dark eye, and a pointed yellow or dark beak. Juveniles are "
    "plain grey-brown with a dark beak.",
    "mourning_dove": "A plump grey-brown dove with a small head, a long pointed tail, and black "
    "spots on the wings.",
    "house_sparrow": "A small streaky brown sparrow. Males have a grey crown and a black bib.",
    "house_finch": "A small streaky brown finch. Males have a rosy red head and chest.",
    "red_winged_blackbird": "A glossy black bird with a red shoulder patch edged in yellow.",
    "downy_woodpecker": "A small black-and-white woodpecker with a white stripe down the back "
    "and spotted wings. Males have a red patch on the back of the head.",
    "other": "A bird that matches none of the other descriptions.",
}

QUESTIONS = {
    "bird_present": Noul(instructions="Is there at least one bird in `frame`?"),
    "how_many": Choice(
        instructions="How many birds are in `frame`?",
        criteria={
            "none": "No bird at all.",
            "one": "Exactly one bird.",
            "several": "Two or more birds.",
        },
    ),
    "bird": Box(instructions="The most prominent bird in `frame`"),
    "species_left": Choice(
        instructions="What species is the leftmost bird in `frame`?", criteria=SPECIES
    ),
    "species_right": Choice(
        instructions="What species is the rightmost bird in `frame`?", criteria=SPECIES
    ),
}
```

## Ask about one frame

Each request sends one frame and a set of questions, with the model version and the images
header set above. The three frames below have two birds, one bird, and no bird.

```python expandable theme={null}
@json_cache
def ask_cached(frame: str, questions_json: str) -> dict:
    started = perf_counter()
    response = client.system_one(
        state={"frame": Image(FRAMES / frame)},
        questions=json.loads(questions_json),
        model=TYPESAFE_MODEL,
        extra_headers=IMAGE_HEADERS,
    )
    seconds = round(perf_counter() - started, 2)
    return {"response": response.model_dump(mode="json", exclude={"model"}), "seconds": seconds}


def ask(path: Path, questions: dict):
    as_json = json.dumps(
        {key: q.model_dump(mode="json", exclude_none=True) for key, q in questions.items()},
        sort_keys=True,
    )
    cached = ask_cached(path.name, as_json)
    # The cache leaves the model out; the response type needs one, so use the requested model.
    response = SystemOneResponse.model_validate({**cached["response"], "model": TYPESAFE_MODEL})
    return response, cached["seconds"]


def edges(box) -> str:
    return f"left {box.left:.2f}  right {box.right:.2f}  top {box.top:.2f}  bottom {box.bottom:.2f}"


def show_first_request(name: str) -> None:
    response, seconds = ask(FRAMES / name, QUESTIONS)
    how_many = response.choices["how_many"]
    print(f"{name}  labeled {labels[name]['species'] or 'empty'}  ({seconds:.2f} s)")
    print(f"  bird_present   {response.nouls['bird_present'].noul:.2f}")
    print(f"  how_many       {how_many.choice} {how_many.probabilities[how_many.choice]:.2f}")
    bird = response.boxes["bird"]
    print(f"  bird           {edges(bird.box)}  confidence {bird.confidence:.2f}")
    for key in ("species_left", "species_right"):
        answer = response.choices[key]
        print(f"  {key:<15}{answer.choice} {answer.probabilities[answer.choice]:.2f}")
    print()


for name in ("u010.jpg", "u090.jpg", "u097.jpg"):
    show_first_request(name)
```

```
u010.jpg  labeled ['cardinal_male', 'downy_woodpecker']  (0.35 s)
  bird_present   0.98
  how_many       several 1.00
  bird           left 0.13  right 0.42  top 0.58  bottom 0.90  confidence 0.71
  species_left   cardinal_male 1.00
  species_right  downy_woodpecker 1.00

u090.jpg  labeled ['downy_woodpecker']  (0.29 s)
  bird_present   0.95
  how_many       one 1.00
  bird           left 0.33  right 0.44  top 0.43  bottom 0.94  confidence 0.85
  species_left   downy_woodpecker 0.99
  species_right  downy_woodpecker 0.99

u097.jpg  labeled empty  (0.28 s)
  bird_present   0.07
  how_many       none 0.99
  bird           left 0.04  right 0.13  top 0.47  bottom 0.80  confidence 0.14
  species_left   other 0.38
  species_right  other 0.61
```

The two-bird frame came back as `several`, with the cardinal on the left, the woodpecker on
the right, and both species answers near 1.00. On the one-bird frame, the left and right
answers both name the woodpecker. On the empty frame, `bird_present` is low, so the code
ignores the box and the species answers. Those answers still name an option, here `other`.

On the two-bird frame, the `bird` box covers only the cardinal. One Box question returns
one box, so the woodpecker needs a question of its own.

## Box each bird by its species

We need two Box questions, one for "the leftmost bird" and one for "the
rightmost bird". On this feeder, both boxes landed on the cardinal.

```python theme={null}
POSITION_BOXES = {
    "leftmost": Box(instructions="The leftmost bird in `frame`"),
    "rightmost": Box(instructions="The rightmost bird in `frame`"),
}
by_position, _ = ask(FRAMES / "u010.jpg", POSITION_BOXES)
for key in POSITION_BOXES:
    answer = by_position.boxes[key]
    print(f"{key:<11}{edges(answer.box)}  confidence {answer.confidence:.2f}")
```

```
leftmost   left 0.13  right 0.42  top 0.58  bottom 0.91  confidence 0.76
rightmost  left 0.13  right 0.41  top 0.40  bottom 0.88  confidence 0.32
```

Both boxes cover the same part of the frame. We need to ask for each bird by its species.
The first request already said which two species are there, so the second request
asks for "the male northern cardinal" and "the downy woodpecker". The phrase for each
species is in `BOX_TARGETS`. Where the name alone could also fit another bird, the phrase
adds what the bird looks like.

```python theme={null}
BOX_TARGETS = {
    "blue_jay": "the blue jay",
    "cardinal_male": "the male northern cardinal (the bright red bird)",
    "cardinal_female": "the female northern cardinal (the brown bird with an orange beak)",
    "grackle": "the common grackle (the glossy black bird)",
    "starling": "the European starling (the speckled dark bird)",
    "mourning_dove": "the mourning dove",
    "house_sparrow": "the house sparrow",
    "house_finch": "the house finch",
    "red_winged_blackbird": "the red-winged blackbird",
    "downy_woodpecker": "the downy woodpecker (the black and white bird)",
    "other": "the bird that is none of the listed species",
}


def box_questions(species: list[str]) -> dict:
    return {sp: Box(instructions=f"{BOX_TARGETS[sp]} in `frame`") for sp in species}


by_species, _ = ask(FRAMES / "u010.jpg", box_questions(["cardinal_male", "downy_woodpecker"]))
for key, answer in by_species.boxes.items():
    print(f"{key:<17}{edges(answer.box)}  confidence {answer.confidence:.2f}")
```

```
cardinal_male    left 0.13  right 0.42  top 0.58  bottom 0.92  confidence 0.84
downy_woodpecker left 0.59  right 0.73  top 0.40  bottom 0.88  confidence 0.36
```

With named boxes, the woodpecker gets its own box, to the right of the cardinal's. Its box
confidence, 0.36, is lower than the cardinal's 0.84. The figure
below shows both pairs of boxes on the frame.

```python expandable theme={null}
SURFACE, INK, INK2, MUTED = "#fcfcfb", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781"
BLUE, ORANGE = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"
COLOURS = {"cardinal_male": ORANGE, "downy_woodpecker": BLUE}  # every other species: INK2
FONT = ImageFont.load_default(size=26)


def draw(ax, name: str, boxes: list[tuple[str, dict, str]], title: str) -> None:
    """Draw (label, edges, colour) boxes on a frame and put it on a matplotlib axis."""
    image = PILImage.open(FRAMES / name).convert("RGB")
    width, height = image.size
    pen = ImageDraw.Draw(image)
    for label, e, colour in boxes:
        x0, y0 = e["left"] * width, e["top"] * height
        pen.rectangle([x0, y0, e["right"] * width, e["bottom"] * height], outline=colour, width=6)
        text_box = pen.textbbox((x0, y0), label, font=FONT)
        y = y0 - (text_box[3] - text_box[1]) - 12 if y0 > 40 else y0 + 6
        pen.rectangle([x0, y, x0 + text_box[2] - text_box[0] + 12, y + 36], fill=colour)
        pen.text((x0 + 6, y + 2), label, fill="white", font=FONT)
    ax.imshow(image)
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=10, color=INK2)


def show(fig, filename: str) -> None:
    """Show a figure in a notebook; save it as a PNG when run as a script."""
    if __name__ == "__main__" and "__file__" in globals():
        fig.savefig(filename, dpi=120)
        print(f"saved {filename}")
    else:
        display(fig)
    plt.close(fig)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), facecolor=SURFACE)
draw(
    axes[0],
    "u010.jpg",
    [(key, by_position.boxes[key].box.model_dump(), MUTED) for key in POSITION_BOXES],
    "Box by position: both boxes on the cardinal",
)
draw(
    axes[1],
    "u010.jpg",
    [(key.replace("_", " "), a.box.model_dump(), COLOURS[key]) for key, a in by_species.boxes.items()],
    "Box by species name: one box per bird",
)
fig.suptitle("The second request on frame u010 (0:09)", x=0.01, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout()
show(fig, "second-request.png")
```

![output](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/l_j5jNYNp6JTBESY/cookbooks/feeder_watch/feeder_watch.executed.1.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=l_j5jNYNp6JTBESY\&q=85\&s=4958af057b8d6595f79deba1a373e01a)

A Box question always returns a box. If the first request names a species that is barely in
the frame, such as a bird hidden behind the feeder, the second request still returns a box
for that species, and the box can land on the other bird. Two named boxes that overlap by
0.6 or more are treated as the same bird found twice, and only the box with the higher
confidence is kept. Overlap here is intersection over union: the area the two boxes share,
divided by the total area they cover.

```python theme={null}
OVERLAP_AT = 0.6  # two named boxes overlapping this much are one bird found twice


def overlap(a: dict, b: dict) -> float:
    """Intersection over union of two boxes given as edge fractions."""
    w = max(0.0, min(a["right"], b["right"]) - max(a["left"], b["left"]))
    h = max(0.0, min(a["bottom"], b["bottom"]) - max(a["top"], b["top"]))
    area = lambda e: (e["right"] - e["left"]) * (e["bottom"] - e["top"])  # noqa: E731
    union = area(a) + area(b) - w * h
    return w * h / union if union > 0 else 0.0


def dedupe(birds: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    kept: list[dict] = []
    for bird in sorted(birds, key=lambda b: -b["box_confidence"]):
        if all(overlap(bird["box"], k["box"]) < OVERLAP_AT for k in kept):
            kept.append(bird)
    return kept
```

## Ask about every frame

For each frame:

1. Send the five questions. Stop there if `bird_present` is below 0.5, or if neither
   species answer reaches 0.5.
2. If `how_many` is `several` and the two species answers name different species, send the
   second request for one box per species, then run `dedupe()` on the boxes. Do the same
   when only one side's answer reaches 0.5, because the `bird` box might be around the
   other bird.
3. Otherwise, keep the most likely species and the `bird` box from the first request.

The result for a frame is each bird's species, species probability, box and box
confidence, plus the number of requests and the seconds the frame took.

```python expandable theme={null}
PRESENT_AT = 0.5  # below this, the frame is empty and the other answers are ignored
SPECIES_AT = 0.5  # a species answer below this is too unsure to name a box


def ask_frame(path: Path) -> dict:
    first, seconds = ask(path, QUESTIONS)
    result = {
        "frame": path.name,
        "bird_present": first.nouls["bird_present"].noul,
        "how_many": first.choices["how_many"].choice,
        "birds": [],
        "requests": 1,
        "seconds": seconds,
    }
    # the species named by the leftmost and rightmost answers, each with its best probability
    named: dict[str, float] = {}
    sure_sides = 0
    for key in ("species_left", "species_right"):
        answer = first.choices[key]
        p = answer.probabilities[answer.choice]
        if p >= SPECIES_AT:
            named[answer.choice] = max(p, named.get(answer.choice, 0.0))
            sure_sides += 1
    if result["bird_present"] < PRESENT_AT or not named:
        return result

    # with several birds, the `bird` box only fits when both sides name the same species
    if result["how_many"] == "several" and (len(named) == 2 or sure_sides < 2):
        second, more_seconds = ask(path, box_questions(list(named)))
        result["requests"] = 2
        result["seconds"] += more_seconds
        boxes = {sp: second.boxes[sp] for sp in named}
    else:
        top = max(named, key=named.get)
        named, boxes = {top: named[top]}, {top: first.boxes["bird"]}

    birds = [
        {"species": sp, "p": p, "box": boxes[sp].box.model_dump(), "box_confidence": boxes[sp].confidence}
        for sp, p in named.items()
    ]
    result["birds"] = dedupe(birds)
    return result
```

The frames don't depend on each other, so four threads ask about them in parallel. The
results still come back in frame order, because `pool.map` keeps the order of its input. On
a live camera, send one frame at a time instead, each as soon as the previous answer is
back.

```python theme={null}
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:  # 101 frames, about 180 requests, 4 at a time
    results = list(pool.map(ask_frame, paths))

two_requests = [r for r in results if r["requests"] == 2]
print(f"{len(results)} frames, {sum(r['requests'] for r in results)} requests")
print(f"frames that needed the second request: {len(two_requests)}")
print(f"frames that ended with two boxes:      {sum(len(r['birds']) == 2 for r in results)}")
print(f"seconds per frame, median: {statistics.median(r['seconds'] for r in results):.2f}")
```

```
101 frames, 178 requests
frames that needed the second request: 77
frames that ended with two boxes:      66
seconds per frame, median: 0.54
```

Some frames sent the second request and still ended with one box. On those frames, either
only one species answer reached 0.5, or the two named boxes overlapped and `dedupe()` kept
one.

## Turn answers into visits

Visits are built from the results in frame order, one species at a time, so two birds at
the feeder at once make two overlapping visits. Three settings decide what counts as a
visit:

* A frame counts toward a species when that species' probability is at least `species_at`.
* A visit stays open through gaps of up to `max_gap` frames, such as when the bird hops out
  of view for a moment.
* A visit needs at least `min_frames` frames that name its species. With the default of 2,
  a wrong answer on a single frame doesn't become a visit.

These settings belong to your application, and Jev never sees them. To try other values,
rerun `visits()` on the saved results. No new requests are needed.

```python expandable theme={null}
def visits(results: list[dict], species_at=0.6, max_gap=2, min_frames=2) -> list[dict]:
    done, open_visits, last_seen = [], {}, {}
    for second, result in enumerate(results):  # one frame per second
        seen = {b["species"] for b in result["birds"] if b["p"] >= species_at}
        for sp in list(open_visits):
            if sp not in seen and second - last_seen[sp] > max_gap:
                done.append(open_visits.pop(sp))
        for sp in sorted(seen):
            if sp in open_visits:
                open_visits[sp]["end"] = second
                open_visits[sp]["frames"] += 1
            else:
                open_visits[sp] = {"species": sp, "start": second, "end": second, "frames": 1}
            last_seen[sp] = second
    done.extend(open_visits.values())
    kept = [v for v in done if v["frames"] >= min_frames]
    return sorted(kept, key=lambda v: (v["start"], v["species"]))


def clock(second: int) -> str:
    return f"{second // 60}:{second % 60:02d}"


def print_visits(found: list[dict]) -> None:
    for v in found:
        seconds = v["end"] - v["start"] + 1
        print(f"  {v['species']:<18}{clock(v['start'])} to {clock(v['end'])}  ({seconds} s)")


found = visits(results)
print("Visits:")
print_visits(found)

per_species: dict[str, list[int]] = {}
for v in found:
    count = per_species.setdefault(v["species"], [0, 0])
    count[0] += 1
    count[1] += v["end"] - v["start"] + 1
print("\nPer species:")
for sp, (n, seconds) in sorted(per_species.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1][1]):
    print(f"  {sp:<18}{n} visit{'s' if n > 1 else ''}, {seconds} s at the feeder")
print("\nVisits in the hand labels:")
print_visits(visits([{"birds": [{"species": s, "p": 1.0} for s in labels[n]["species"]]} for n in NAMES]))
```

```
Visits:
  cardinal_male     0:00 to 1:02  (63 s)
  downy_woodpecker  0:00 to 1:29  (90 s)
  cardinal_male     1:12 to 1:15  (4 s)

Per species:
  downy_woodpecker  1 visit, 90 s at the feeder
  cardinal_male     2 visits, 67 s at the feeder

Visits in the hand labels:
  cardinal_male     0:00 to 1:02  (63 s)
  downy_woodpecker  0:00 to 1:29  (90 s)
```

As a timeline, each row of the visit log is a species and each bar is one visit, with the
total time at the feeder beside the row.

```python expandable theme={null}
def draw_visits(found: list[dict], seconds: int, title: str) -> None:
    by_species: dict[str, list[dict]] = {}
    for v in found:
        by_species.setdefault(v["species"], []).append(v)
    total = {sp: sum(v["end"] - v["start"] + 1 for v in vs) for sp, vs in by_species.items()}
    order = sorted(by_species, key=lambda sp: -total[sp])

    height = 0.45 * len(order) + 1.4
    fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(
        1, 2, figsize=(11, height), facecolor=SURFACE,
        gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [3.6, 1], "wspace": 0.04},
    )
    for a in (ax, bx):
        a.set_facecolor(SURFACE)
        a.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
        a.tick_params(colors=INK2, labelsize=9, length=0)
    for row, sp in enumerate(order):
        colour = MUTED if sp == "other" else BLUE
        spans = [(v["start"], v["end"] - v["start"] + 1) for v in by_species[sp]]
        ax.broken_barh(spans, (row - 0.32, 0.64), facecolors=colour)
        bx.barh(row, total[sp], height=0.64, color=colour)
        n = len(by_species[sp])
        label = f"{total[sp]} s, {n} visit{'s' if n > 1 else ''}"
        bx.text(total[sp] + seconds * 0.03, row, label, va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)), [sp.replace("_", " ") for sp in order], color=INK, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlim(0, seconds)
    ax.set_xticks(range(0, seconds + 1, 10), [clock(s) for s in range(0, seconds + 1, 10)])
    ax.grid(axis="x", color="#e4e3df")
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.set_title("Each visit, by time of footage (m:ss)", loc="left", fontsize=10, color=INK2)
    bx.set_xlim(0, seconds * 1.6)
    bx.set_xticks([])
    bx.set_yticks([])
    bx.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
    bx.set_title("Time at the feeder", loc="left", fontsize=10, color=INK2)
    for a in (ax, bx):
        a.set_ylim(len(order) - 0.5, -0.5)
    fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=12, color=INK)
    # margins in inches: the species names on the left, the titles on top, the times below
    fig.subplots_adjust(left=1.6 / 11, right=0.99, top=1 - 0.75 / height, bottom=0.4 / height)
    show(fig, "visits.png")


draw_visits(found, len(results), f"{len(found)} visits in {clock(len(results))} of footage")
```

The two long visits match the visit log built the same way from our hand labels, with the
same start and end seconds. In every run we made of this clip, the two long visits came out
the same, but the short visits changed from run to run.

The short visit here is wrong: the male cardinal visit from 1:12 to 1:15 is a female
cardinal behind the feeder, misnamed when only her red beak showed.

Lowering `min_frames` to 1 shows the single-frame sightings that the default of 2 keeps out
of the log:

```python theme={null}
logged = {(v["species"], v["start"]) for v in visits(results)}
print("Single-frame sightings that min_frames=2 leaves out:")
print_visits([v for v in visits(results, min_frames=1) if (v["species"], v["start"]) not in logged])
```

```
Single-frame sightings that min_frames=2 leaves out:
  cardinal_female   1:04 to 1:04  (1 s)
  cardinal_female   1:08 to 1:08  (1 s)
  other             1:16 to 1:16  (1 s)
  cardinal_male     1:34 to 1:34  (1 s)
```

Some of these are real birds, such as the female cardinal at 1:04 and 1:08, and some are
misreads, such as the male cardinal at 1:34. A higher `min_frames` keeps more wrong answers
out of the log, and it also drops more birds that only show up for a second or two.

## Check the answers against the labels

Two checks compare the answers with the hand labels:

* whether `bird_present` agrees with the label on whether the frame has a bird in it
* whether every labeled bird's species is among the species that `ask_frame()` returned

A frame marked `partial` counts as having a bird for the first check. It is left out of the
second, because its label doesn't name every bird in it.

```python theme={null}
present_ok, found, total, misses = 0, 0, 0, []
for r in results:
    label = labels[r["frame"]]
    has_bird = bool(label["species"]) or label["partial"]  # a partial bird is still a bird
    if (r["bird_present"] >= PRESENT_AT) == has_bird:
        present_ok += 1
    else:
        misses.append(f"{r['frame']}  bird_present {r['bird_present']:.2f}, labeled {label['species'] or 'empty'}")
    if label["partial"]:
        continue
    returned = {b["species"] for b in r["birds"]}
    for sp in label["species"]:
        total += 1
        if sp in returned:
            found += 1
        else:
            misses.append(f"{r['frame']}  labeled {sp}, returned {sorted(returned) or 'nothing'}")

print(f"bird_present agrees with the labels: {present_ok}/{len(results)} frames")
print(f"labeled birds returned:              {found}/{total}")
print("\nDisagreements:")
print("\n".join(misses) or "none")
```

```
bird_present agrees with the labels: 101/101 frames
labeled birds returned:              132/133

Disagreements:
u063.jpg  labeled downy_woodpecker, returned ['cardinal_male']
```

The hardest frames for `bird_present` are 1:33 and 1:34, where only part of a cardinal
shows; the left half of the figure below is 1:33. Jev scored both at about 0.8 and counted
the bird, and the labels mark both `partial`.

The one labeled bird that Jev missed is the woodpecker at 1:02, which shares the frame with
the male cardinal. That frame came back with only the male cardinal.

The right half of the figure shows a failure that `dedupe()` doesn't catch. At 1:15, the
female cardinal's beak shows at the right edge of the cage, and Jev named a male cardinal.
The box for the male cardinal landed on the woodpecker. It overlaps the woodpecker's own
box by less than 0.6, so both boxes stay. A check on each box would catch this: crop to the
box and ask a `Noul` question whether the bird in the crop is a male cardinal.

```python theme={null}
by_frame = {r["frame"]: r for r in results}


def answer_boxes(name: str) -> list[tuple[str, dict, str]]:
    return [
        (f"{b['species'].replace('_', ' ')} {b['p']:.2f}", b["box"], COLOURS.get(b["species"], INK2))
        for b in by_frame[name]["birds"]
    ]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6), facecolor=SURFACE)
for ax, name in zip(axes, ("u094.jpg", "u076.jpg")):
    r = by_frame[name]
    second = int(name[1:4]) - 1
    draw(ax, name, answer_boxes(name), f"{clock(second)}  bird_present {r['bird_present']:.2f}")
fig.suptitle("Two hard frames from the run", x=0.01, ha="left", color=INK, fontsize=12)
fig.tight_layout()
show(fig, "failures.png")
```

## See it running live

The same questions work on live footage. The video below shows a small web app built on
them. It takes a frame from a webcam or a video file, asks Jev,
draws the boxes, and keeps a running visit log. In the video, it plays a stretch of the
Ostdrossel feeder cam that the questions weren't tuned on, at about two answers a second.

[Feeder watch web app demo](https://player.vimeo.com/video/1237184729)

Bird footage: [Ostdrossel feeder cam](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h6iNvPiyPbI) by
Ostdrossel, licensed [CC BY](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), shown with
boxes and labels added by the app.

## Before you point it at your own camera

* **One Box question returns one box.** This code boxes at most two birds per frame,
  and only when they are different species. For more species, ask one `Noul` question per
  species, such as "Is there a blue jay in `frame`?", then a named Box for each species
  whose answer comes back high.
* **Two birds of the same species can't be told apart by name.** For a flock, a zero-shot
  detector such as Meta's SAM 3 can find every bird from the text prompt "bird", with no
  training. Jev can then name the species of each cropped bird.
* **Small frames are rejected.** The [Images](/images) page allows 280 to 1568 pixels on
  each side, with at least 78,400 pixels in total (280 × 280).
* **Adjust the thresholds as needed.** The values of `PRESENT_AT`, `SPECIES_AT`,
  `OVERLAP_AT`, and the `visits()` defaults worked here. Label a few minutes of your own
  footage and check them against it.
* **Write the species list for your camera.** Describe what your camera shows of each bird,
  close-ups included. Keep the `other` option, so that a bird your list doesn't name isn't
  forced into one of the names it does have.


# Function calling
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling

Turns natural-language trading requests into calls to ordinary typed functions by mapping function names and closed-set arguments to confidence-aware System One questions.

When you order a "large iced oat latte, no sweetener," the barista does not write your
sentence down. They mark four options on a cup. This cookbook does the same thing for
a trading API: a sentence goes in, and out comes a function name and its arguments as
evaluated enums, each with a confidence.

```text theme={null}
"plot rolling correlation between nvda and spy for the past month"
    rolling_correlation(symbol='NVDA', benchmark='SPY', window='1mo')   confidence 0.91

"compare nvda amd and msft over the past three months"
    compare_returns(symbols=['NVDA', 'AMD', 'MSFT'], window='3mo')      confidence 0.94

"show me apple daily with volume"
    plot_price(symbol='AAPL', resolution='1d', include_volume=True)     confidence 0.75

"what tickers do you have"
    list_symbols()                                                     confidence 1.00
```

Those calls go to ten ordinary functions in a trading assistant. Their arguments take
values from fixed lists, so they are `Literal`s already:

```python theme={null}
def plot_price(
    symbol: Literal["SPY", "NVDA", "AMD", "AAPL", "MSFT", "TSLA"],
    style: Literal["line", "candles"] = "line",
    resolution: Literal["1m", "5m", "15m", "1h", "1d"] = "15m",
    window: Literal["1d", "1w", "1mo", "3mo"] = "1w",
    include_volume: bool = False,
    moving_average: Literal["9", "20", "50"] | None = None,
    log_scale: bool = False,
): ...
```

An argument whose values come from a fixed list is a closed set. When it takes one value
out of that list, it gets a `Choice` question over exactly those values, so whatever
reaches the function is a value the function accepts. You leave the functions alone. What
you add is a spec that says in plain words what each argument means. By the end you have a
`Dispatcher` you can point at your own functions.

## Setup

```bash theme={null}
pip install ipython polars matplotlib numpy 'cooksafe>=0.2.0,<0.3.0'
```

Set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. The code below downloads two modules, with `spec.json` and the
price bars, from
[typesafe-public-examples](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/tree/main/cookbooks/function_calling)
unless they are already on disk. `trader.py` holds the ten functions, plus a TypeSafe
client that caches its answers. `dispatch.py` holds the code that reads a signature and a
spec and makes the call.

The prices are simulated from a fixed random seed, not real market data. The tickers are
real, but every price, return and chart below is generated.

```python theme={null}

        urllib.request.urlretrieve(f"{EXAMPLES}/{name}", name)

from dispatch import ROUTE, Dispatcher, closed_sets  # noqa: E402  (downloaded above)
from trader import TOOLS, client, load  # noqa: E402
```

## Find the closed sets in the signatures

The type hints already say which arguments come from a fixed list, and what is in each
list. `closed_sets` reads a signature and sorts those arguments into three shapes: a
**choice** (a `Literal`, so one value out of the list), a **set** (a `list[Literal[...]]`,
so any number of them), or a **flag** (a `bool`, so on or off). All ten functions are
defined in `trader.py`.

```python theme={null}
for name, fn in TOOLS.items():
    shapes = closed_sets(fn)
    print(
        f"  {name:<20}{len(shapes)}  "
        + ", ".join(f"{a}:{s}" for a, (s, _) in shapes.items())
    )
print(
    f"\n{sum(len(closed_sets(fn)) for fn in TOOLS.values())} fillable arguments in total"
)
```

```
  list_symbols        0  
  market_summary      1  window:choice
  plot_price          7  symbol:choice, style:choice, resolution:choice, window:choice, include_volume:flag, moving_average:choice, log_scale:flag
  intraday_pattern    3  symbol:choice, window:choice, metric:choice
  compare_returns     3  symbols:set, window:choice, normalize:flag
  rolling_correlation 4  symbol:choice, benchmark:choice, window:choice, resolution:choice
  summary_stats       2  symbol:choice, window:choice
  volatility          3  symbol:choice, window:choice, annualized:flag
  top_movers          2  window:choice, direction:choice
  drawdown            3  symbol:choice, window:choice, plot:flag

28 fillable arguments in total
```

`top_movers` shows what gets left out. Of its three arguments, two are closed sets. The
third, `limit`, is an `int`, so it never gets a question and keeps its default of 3. Free
text, numbers and dates work the same way: no question, and the function's default stands.

## Write the spec

The `Literal` gives you the strings `"1mo"` and `"3mo"`. It does not say that a user typing
"this quarter" means the second one. The spec says that. It holds a question per argument,
a line per option, a description per function, and one more question that picks between the
functions. It lives in `spec.json`, and an LLM can write it for you from the signatures.

```python theme={null}
SPEC = json.loads(Path("spec.json").read_text())
for argument in ("style", "moving_average"):
    print(
        json.dumps(
            {argument: SPEC["functions"]["plot_price"]["arguments"][argument]}, indent=2
        )
    )
```

```
{
  "style": {
    "question": "Does the user want a plain line or candles?",
    "stated": "Does the user say how the chart should be drawn, such as a line, candles, or OHLC bars?",
    "options": {
      "line": "a simple line through the closing prices",
      "candles": "a candlestick or OHLC chart, showing each bar's open, high, low and close"
    }
  }
}
{
  "moving_average": {
    "question": "How many bars should the moving average cover - nine, twenty, or fifty?",
    "stated": "Does the user ask for a moving average or a smoothed line over the candles?",
    "options": {
      "9": "a nine-bar moving average, a fast one",
      "20": "a twenty-bar moving average",
      "50": "a fifty-bar moving average, a slow one"
    }
  }
}
```

The option keys are the strings the function takes, so nothing has to map a label back to
an argument afterwards. `stated` makes an argument optional. It is a second yes/no question
asking whether the command says anything about that argument at all. When the answer is no,
the call leaves that argument out and the function's own default applies.

A set argument gets its question once per member, with `{}` standing in for the member
name. `"Does the user want {} in the comparison?"` becomes one question per ticker.

Write each question about the idea rather than the words a user might pick, because the
match is on meaning: "is amd tracking nvidia lately" reaches `rolling_correlation` even
though neither *tracking* nor *lately* appears anywhere in `spec.json`. Avoid naming a
question after its parameter - `"Which resolution?"` gives the command nothing to match
against.

## Turn the spec into questions

`Dispatcher` builds the questions from the spec once. Each command is then one request
carrying the choice of function and every function's arguments, and the dispatcher reads
only the chosen function's answers.

```python theme={null}
assistant = Dispatcher(SPEC, TOOLS, client)
print(f"{len(assistant.questions)} questions per command, among them:")
for qid in (
    "__tool__",
    "plot_price.style",
    "plot_price.style?",
    "compare_returns.symbols.NVDA",
):
    question = assistant.questions[qid]
    print(f"  {qid:<30}{question['type']:<8}{str(question['instructions'])[:64]}")
```

```
54 questions per command, among them:
  __tool__                      choice  What is the user asking the trading assistant to do?
  plot_price.style              choice  Does the user want a plain line or candles?
  plot_price.style?             noul    Does the user say how the chart should be drawn, such as a line,
  compare_returns.symbols.NVDA  noul    Does the user want NVDA in the comparison?
```

## Run fourteen commands

A request occupies one line, and its `confidence` is the least certain judgement behind
that call.

```python theme={null}
COMMANDS = [
    "show nvda 1h",
    "plot rolling correlation between nvda and spy for the past month",
    "when during the day does nvda trade the most",
    "what moved today",
    "what tickers do you have",
    "how did the market do this week",
    "candles for tesla with a 20 period moving average",
    "compare nvda amd and msft over the past three months",
    "how volatile is tsla",
    "biggest losers today",
    "worst drawdown for nvda this quarter, and chart it please",
    "spy stats for the last month",
    "show me apple daily with volume",
    "is amd tracking nvidia lately",
]

CALLS = {command: assistant(command) for command in COMMANDS}
for command, call in CALLS.items():
    print(f'  "{command}"')
    print(
        f"      {str(call):<66}confidence {call.confidence:.2f}"
        f"   tool {call.tool.probability:.2f}"
    )
```

Both long commands came out as asked. "plot rolling correlation between nvda and spy for
the past month" filled four arguments from one sentence. Two of them, `symbol` and
`benchmark`, draw from the same six tickers, and each ticker landed in the right argument
because the questions spell out the roles: *the one being measured, named first* against
*the second one named, the yardstick*. "compare nvda amd and msft over the past three
months" put three tickers in the set and left the other three out.

Running three of them:

```python theme={null}
for command in ("how did the market do this week", "biggest losers today"):
    print(f'"{command}"  ->  {CALLS[command]}')
    print(CALLS[command].run(), "\n")
```

## Read the confidence

`confidence` reports the least certain judgement in the call, rather than the product of
all of them, since one wrong argument is enough to spoil the result. A product answers a
different question ("is every part right"), and it falls as a function takes more
arguments, whether or not any one judgement is shaky.

Where that number came from, argument by argument:

```python theme={null}
call = CALLS["is amd tracking nvidia lately"]
print(f'"is amd tracking nvidia lately"  ->  {call}   confidence {call.confidence:.2f}')
for name, argument in call.arguments.items():
    top = sorted(argument.distribution.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:3]
    shown = "omitted, default stands" if argument.omitted else repr(argument.value)
    print(
        f"  {name:<12}{shown:<26}p {argument.probability:.2f}   "
        + "  ".join(f"{k} {v:.2f}" for k, v in top)
    )
print(f"  weakest argument: {call.weakest().name}")
```

```
"is amd tracking nvidia lately"  ->  rolling_correlation(symbol='AMD', benchmark='NVDA')   confidence 0.82
  symbol      'AMD'                     p 0.87   AMD 0.87  NVDA 0.13  AAPL 0.00
  benchmark   'NVDA'                    p 0.78   NVDA 0.92  AMD 0.08  AAPL 0.00
  window      omitted, default stands   p 0.96   
  resolution  omitted, default stands   p 0.99   
  weakest argument: benchmark
```

`window` and `resolution` are both omitted here, because "lately" does not say how far back
or on what bars, so `rolling_correlation` runs on its own defaults of one month and hourly
bars. That is what the `stated` question is for. Without it, the choice would have to name
some window, and it would have named one confidently.

# Hierarchical classification
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification

Uses parallel beam search over Jev's Choice probabilities to classify documents in deep patent, retail product, and biomedical hierarchies.

Many kinds of data are hierarchies: taxonomies, file systems, websites, codebases, org
charts, biological ontologies, LLM skills and moderation policies. Hierarchical
classification walks a hierarchy from the root to the correct leaf node; that leaf is the
final classification. We start at the root, ask a System One `Choice` question over its
children, follow the most probable child, and repeat until we reach a leaf
(**Greedy Search**).

Because System One questions can run in parallel, we can also follow several paths at once
with **Beam Search**, so one wrong early choice doesn't decide the result. At each level,
beam search scores every path by the geometric mean of its edge probabilities,
`product(edge_probabilities) ** (1 / decisions)`, keeps the best `K`, and prunes the rest.
The geometric mean, unlike the raw product, doesn't penalize a deep leaf just for taking
more decisions.

Asking one question per node also helps you observe and test the classifier:

* Observability
  * identify which nodes your misclassifications occur most in
  * measure the number of times each node and edge is traversed
* Testability
  * unit test and measure the impact of hierarchy updates on classification performance

### Hierarchies used in this cookbook

* **[CPC 2026.05](https://www.cooperativepatentclassification.org/):** patent subject
  matter, from broad technology sections to narrow inventions. Published by the European
  Patent Office and the US Patent and Trademark Office.
* **[Shopify 2026-02](https://github.com/Shopify/product-taxonomy):** retail product
  categories, from store departments to specific product types. From Shopify's Product
  Taxonomy (MIT).
* **[MeSH 2026](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/):** biomedical subjects from broad domains to
  specific conditions. MeSH is a DAG, so one descriptor can appear under several parents;
  we give each of its official tree numbers a separate path. Source: U.S. National Library
  of Medicine. This is the January 2026 build of MeSH 2026 and may not be the most current
  MeSH data.

Attribution and licences for the three are in
[`DATA_LICENSE.md`](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-public-examples/blob/main/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification/DATA_LICENSE.md).

### Methods

* **Greedy search:** choose the highest-probability child and discard every alternative.
  One early mistake cannot be recovered.
* **Beam search:** retain `K` plausible paths and classify every frontier in parallel.
  When an early choice is close, a clearer decision further down can put the right path
  back on top. The leaf of the path with the highest geometric-mean probability is the
  final classification.
* **System One Choice questions:** each node asks one `Choice` question over its children,
  and the answer's probabilities become the edge probabilities. The beam's `K` questions
  at each level run in parallel, so beam search takes one round of calls per level, as
  greedy search does.
* **Formula:**
  * `path_score = product(edge_probabilities) ** (1 / decisions)`
    * used for pruning and comparing paths
    * for hierarchies deeper than about 10 levels, compute it as `exp(mean(log(probs)))`
      to avoid floating-point precision loss
  * `separation = top_path_score / second_path_score`
    * reported only, not used for pruning
    * near `1×`, the top two paths are almost tied; the further above `1×`, the clearer
      the winner
