# Smart home assistant demo
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/demos/smart-home

Demo code: a smart home assistant that uses Jev to evaluate user requests.

## Check it out in action

[Smart home assistant demo video](https://player.vimeo.com/video/1230923853)

## How it works

### Speculative fan-out

The chief pattern demonstrated here is [speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out). Each user request is evaluated against a long list of questions, including many that will end up irrelevant for most requests.

Let's consider the following user request:

> "Turn off all of the lights in the house"

This is a very simple request, and our code will only need to consider the answers to the following questions:

* "What category of request is this?" (smarthome command)
* "What domain is this request targeting?" (whole house)
* "What type of device is this request targeting?" (lights)
* "What action should be taken on the lights?" (turn off)

Notice that the last question is written with the assumption that the user is issuing a command to lights, and we ask it before we know what the user is actually requesting. This is what we call a "speculative question" - we ask it before we even know if it's relevant, allowing us to evaluate all questions in parallel and rely on code to filter out the irrelevant results after the fact. This is a key pattern for building systems that can handle a wide variety of user requests with a single set of questions.

#### The wrong way: sequential API calls

The wrong way to do this would be to separate the questions in to multiple API calls, waiting to ask questions only once you are certain you need the answer:

* "What category of request is this?" (smarthome command)

Then, only once you know it's a smarthome command:

* "What domain is this request targeting?" (whole house)
* "What type of device is this request targeting?" (lights)

Then, only once you know it's targeting lights:

* "What action should be taken on the lights?" (turn off)

This approach optimizes for a minimum number of questions, but it ends up being much slower and more expensive than batching all of the questions in to one upfront API call.

### Jev and LLM pairing

This demo also shows how Jev can be paired with LLMs to handle a system that sometimes requires a string-generation step:

**Splitting a compound user request:** One of the questions in this demo is a Noul question identifying if the user request is asking for more than one distinct action. If this is true, the system uses an LLM to split the request into a list of atomic commands. The split requests are then evaluated by Jev individually.

**Falling back to a conversational LLM:** When Jev determines that the user query is a request for general information or conversation, the system calls an LLM to generate a freeform response. This allows an interactive system to handle requests with known deterministic behavior in a fast and cost efficient way, while still allowing for the flexibility provided by a generative LLM when needed. Jev's initial response is so fast compared to the LLM response that it adds negligible latency to the overall system.

## Run it yourself

This demo is a simple Vite/React single-page app that uses the TypeSafe API to evaluate user requests. The full source code will be available on GitHub at release. Its README includes instructions for running the demo locally and an overview of which bits of the source code are responsible for which parts of the demo.


# Images
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/images

Send images in a System One request: in the state, inside a question's instructions, and as the criteria a question is judged against.

**Dreamer-ready.** Images and Box questions aren't yet up to our standards to call ready for production, but we're excited for dreamers and builders to play with them. Use them to build prototypes and try ideas. The request format, the answers, and the limits on this page can change between releases, and accuracy will change as we update the models. Tell us what you build, and what breaks, on [Discord](https://discord.gg/typesafe).

To use images or Box questions, send the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true` header with each request that contains an image or a Box question. See [Turning on images](/images#turning-on-images).

An image can go anywhere text can go in a System One request: in the `state`, in a question's `instructions`, and in its `criteria`. Every question type accepts images, and the [Box](/primitives/box) question type returns where something is in an image.

![A request body with three references highlighted, each linked to the image it stands for: door.jpg is the camera value in the state, badge.jpg is inside a Noul question's instructions, and thumb.jpg is the value of the thumbs\_up option in a Choice question's criteria. The images themselves are listed in the request's assets.](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/OmOS-OoUA_8VxwSR/images/images/anatomy-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=OmOS-OoUA_8VxwSR\&q=85\&s=7d5e99842cb8a482309f65a6d4aa195e)

## Turning on images

Images and [Box](/primitives/box) questions are off by default. To use them, send the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true` header with each request that contains an image or a Box question. The examples under [Uploading images](#uploading-images) show how. The other examples on this page show only the request body.

## Sending images in a request

Each image is listed once, in the request's top-level `assets` map. Its key in that map is a reference string. Write the reference wherever the image belongs, as a whole string value or inside a longer string, and the model receives the image in its place.

This request sends a photo of a found dog as the state, and puts the photo from a lost-dog poster directly into one question:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-latest",
  "state": {
    "photo": "a3f1c2e8-found"
  },
  "assets": {
    "a3f1c2e8-found": {"type": "image", "format": "jpg", "data_base64": "/9j/4AAQSkZJRg..."},
    "77b0d4a1-poster": {"type": "image", "format": "jpg", "data_base64": "/9j/4AAQSkZJRg..."}
  },
  "questions": {
    "same_dog": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Is the dog in `photo` the same dog as in this picture: 77b0d4a1-poster?"
    },
    "has_collar": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Is the dog in `photo` wearing a collar?"
    },
    "coat": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "What is the coat of the dog in `photo` like?",
      "criteria": {
        "short": "Short and smooth.",
        "long": "Long or feathered.",
        "curly": "Curly or wiry."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Questions can refer to an image in the state by name or path in backticks, the same way they refer to any other field (see [Reference specific fields](/primitives#reference-specific-fields)). An image that only one question uses goes directly in that question's `instructions` or `criteria`, as the poster photo does above.

Jev 1.13 and Jev 1.14 both accept images. [Box](/primitives/box) questions need Jev 1.14.

### Asset fields

**assets** `map\<string, Asset\>`

The images in the request, keyed by reference string. Every reference must appear somewhere in the `state`, `instructions`, or `criteria`.

**Asset properties**

**type** `"image"`

The kind of asset. Optional. If you send it, it must be `"image"`.

**part** `string`

In a multipart request, the name of the file part that holds the image. See [Uploading images](#uploading-images).

**data\_base64** `string`

The image file, base64-encoded. Required unless `part` is set. Use the standard base64 alphabet with `=` padding, no line breaks or other whitespace, and no `data:` prefix.

**format** `"png" | "jpg" | "jpeg"`

The image's format, in lowercase. Required with `data_base64`. Optional with `part`. `"jpeg"` is another name for `"jpg"`.

Send each image one way, with `part` or `data_base64`. If an asset has both, the API uses `part`.

### References

References are matched as plain text anywhere in the request's strings, so a reference works mid-sentence as well as as a whole value. A short reference such as `cat` could also match inside `category`. Use references that can't occur in your text by accident. A new UUID for each image in each request is the safest choice.

* **Every asset must be referenced.** A request with an asset that is not referenced anywhere returns `400`.
* **Whole values match first.** A string that is exactly a reference becomes that image. In longer strings, references are replaced from left to right, and matches never overlap.
* **Each use adds the image again.** The file is uploaded once, but every place its reference appears adds another copy of the image to what the model reads, and every copy counts toward the [expanded request limit](#limits).
* **Object keys are not replaced.** A Choice option name, a question ID, or any other object key stays text. To define a Choice option with a picture, put the reference in the option's description, as in [Criteria](#criteria).
* **Answers contain the reference, not the image,** wherever they repeat your criteria, such as a Score's `legend`.
* **Keep keys short.** Each reference can be at most 1,024 bytes of UTF-8, and all references in a request together at most 65,536 bytes. These limits count bytes, not characters. A reference can't be empty or only whitespace.

The Python and JavaScript SDKs create references for you. See [Uploading images](#uploading-images).

## Uploading images

With the latest Python or JavaScript SDK, put an image object anywhere text can go. The SDK creates a reference for it and uploads the file. This example sends one doorbell photo as the state and asks two questions about it:

```python Python theme={null}
from pathlib import Path

from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Image, Noul, TypeSafeClient

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    result = client.system_one(
        state={"door": Image(Path("door-camera.jpg"))},
        questions={
            "person_present": Noul(instructions="Is there a person in `door`?"),
            "carrying": Choice(
                instructions="What is the person in `door` carrying?",
                criteria={
                    "package": "A box or parcel.",
                    "bag": "A bag of groceries or shopping.",
                    "nothing": "Empty hands.",
                },
            ),
        },
        extra_headers={"TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images": "true"},
    )
    print(result.answers)
```

```typescript JavaScript theme={null}
import { openAsBlob } from "node:fs";
import { choice, image, noul, TypeSafeClient } from "@typesafe-ai/sdk";

const client = new TypeSafeClient();
const door = image(await openAsBlob("door-camera.jpg"));

const { answers } = await client.systemOne(
  {
    state: { door },
    questions: {
      person_present: noul("Is there a person in `door`?"),
      carrying: choice("What is the person in `door` carrying?", {
        package: "A box or parcel.",
        bag: "A bag of groceries or shopping.",
        nothing: "Empty hands.",
      }),
    },
  },
  { headers: { "TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images": "true" } },
);
console.log(answers);
```

To put an image inside a sentence, or to choose your own references, see the [SDK guides](/sdk).

### Over HTTP

Without an SDK, send each image as a file part in a `multipart/form-data` request. Multipart is the better choice: it sends the file as it is, while base64 makes each image about a third larger, and that extra size counts toward the 32 MiB [request body limit](#limits). Base64-encode images into the JSON only when you can't send multipart.

> [tab] Multipart (recommended)
>
> Send the JSON body as the first part, named `request`, with content type `application/json`. Send each image as its own file part, and set that image's `part` in `assets` to the file part's name:
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> curl https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone \
>   -H "Authorization: Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY" \
>   -H "TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true" \
>   -F 'request={
>     "model": "jev-latest",
>     "state": {"door": "a3f1c2e8-door"},
>     "assets": {"a3f1c2e8-door": {"type": "image", "part": "door-photo"}},
>     "questions": {
>       "person_present": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is there a person in `door`?"}
>     }
>   };type=application/json' \
>   -F 'door-photo=@door-camera.jpg;type=image/jpeg'
> ```
>
> The rules for multipart requests:
>
> * The first part is named `request` and holds the JSON body.
> * Part names are unique and not empty. `request` is reserved for the JSON body.
> * Each image part has content type `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/jpg`, or `application/octet-stream`, or no content type. Any other content type returns `400`.
> * Each file part belongs to exactly one asset. A part that no asset names, two assets that name the same part, and an asset whose part is missing all return `400`.
>
> To use the same image in several places, write its reference in each of them.

> [tab] Base64 in JSON
>
> Base64-encode the file into `data_base64` and set `format`, following the rules in [Asset fields](#asset-fields). Python's `base64.b64encode` produces the right encoding. This Python example sends one photo and asks two questions about it:
>
> ```python theme={null}
> import base64
> import os
> import uuid
>
> import requests
>
> def image_asset(path: str) -> tuple[str, dict]:
>     """Return a new reference and the asset entry for one image file."""
>     fmt = "png" if path.lower().endswith(".png") else "jpg"
>     with open(path, "rb") as f:
>         data = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("ascii")
>     return str(uuid.uuid4()), {"type": "image", "format": fmt, "data_base64": data}
>
> photo_key, photo = image_asset("door-camera.jpg")
>
> response = requests.post(
>     "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone",
>     headers={
>         "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['TYPESAFE_API_KEY']}",
>         "TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images": "true",
>     },
>     json={
>         "model": "jev-latest",
>         "state": {"door": photo_key},
>         "assets": {photo_key: photo},
>         "questions": {
>             "person_present": {
>                 "type": "noul",
>                 "instructions": "Is there a person in `door`?",
>             },
>             "carrying": {
>                 "type": "choice",
>                 "instructions": "What is the person in `door` carrying?",
>                 "criteria": {
>                     "package": "A box or parcel.",
>                     "bag": "A bag of groceries or shopping.",
>                     "nothing": "Empty hands.",
>                 },
>             },
>         },
>     },
> )
> print(response.json()["answers"])
> ```

## Image placement

### State

Images in the `state` are part of the state, the same as any text or JSON there. The model evaluates them together with the rest of the state, and every question in the request is evaluated against them. A state can mix images with text, and can hold several images, labeled or nested like any other state data. This state holds a short history of camera frames, oldest first:

```json theme={null}
{
  "state": {
    "frames": [
      {"seconds_ago": 2, "frame": "5c0e9a12-f1"},
      {"seconds_ago": 1, "frame": "1d7be0c4-f2"},
      {"seconds_ago": 0, "frame": "e48a6f30-f3"}
    ]
  }
}
```

A question can ask "Did the door in `frames` open during these frames?" or refer to one frame by path, such as `` `frames[2].frame` ``.

### Instructions

An image in a question's `instructions` is part of that question and is sent only with that question. Put the reference in the sentence where the question needs the image:

```json theme={null}
{
  "state": {"door": "e48a6f30-door"},
  "questions": {
    "is_badge_holder": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Is the person in `door` the same person as in this badge photo: 9a21c7d3-badge?"
    }
  }
}
```

An image in `instructions` is sent to the model once for every question that includes it. When several questions use the same image, put it in the `state` once and refer to it by path from each question. That uses fewer tokens and less of the [size limits](#limits).

### Criteria

Choice options, Score levels, and Noul `true` and `false` definitions can each include images. This Choice classifies a hand gesture, with each option defined by example pictures. The option names are the values your code receives in `choice`, and the pictures are what the model compares the hand against:

```json theme={null}
{
  "state": {"camera": "e48a6f30-cam"},
  "questions": {
    "gesture": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which gesture is the hand in `camera` making?",
      "criteria": {
        "thumbs_up": "0b6c51aa-thumb",
        "open_palm": {
          "description": "A hand held up with the palm facing the camera.",
          "examples": ["4fd2e7b9-palm1", "c83a0e15-palm2"]
        },
        "fist": "a7e94d02-fist",
        "none": "No hand, or a hand that matches none of the examples."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

An option can be an image on its own (`thumbs_up`), a description with one or more examples (`open_palm`), or text only (`none`). The `description` and `examples` keys are names chosen for this example, not required fields: criteria accept any [structure](#structured-data).

Score and Noul criteria take images the same way:

* **Score levels** can each include an example picture. A Score for how open a hand is could use a closed fist, a half-open hand, and an open hand as its three levels.
* **Noul criteria** can define `true` and `false` with pictures: `{"true": {"description": "Correctly assembled", "examples": ["<reference>"]}, "false": "Parts missing or in the wrong place."}`.

### Structured data

State, instructions, and criteria accept nested JSON [structure](/primitives/advanced), and a reference works at any level of it. A question can refer to one picture in an array as `` `lineup[2]` ``, or to one in a labeled object as `` `faces.happy` ``. A criterion can hold several example pictures as an array.

## Patterns

| Pattern | How it works | Where the image goes |
| - | - | - |
| Compare against a known picture | Ask whether the state shows the same person, product, or place as a known picture. | Known picture in `instructions`, photo in `state` |
| Define options by example | Define each Choice option with one or a few example pictures. | `criteria` |
| What changed | Send the previous frame or a short frame history, and ask about motion, arrivals, or differences. | `state` |
| Look closer when needed | Ask about a small copy of the image first. Send a larger copy (up to the size limit), or a full-resolution crop, only when the answer needs more detail. | `state` |
| Search a large image | Cut the image into tiles and ask a Choice with the tiles as its options. Repeat on the chosen tile until the target takes up most of the tile. | `criteria` |
| Find where it is | Ask a [Box](/primitives/box) question for the edges of the target. | `state`, optionally a picture of the target in `instructions` |

## Limits

| Limit | Value |
| - | - |
| Format | PNG or JPEG, still images only. Animated PNGs are rejected. |
| File size | 16 MiB per image file. For base64, this is the size after decoding. |
| Width and height | 280 to 1568 pixels each. An image with either side under 280 pixels is rejected. |
| Total pixels (width × height) | 78,400 to 2,458,624, the area of a 280 × 280 to a 1568 × 1568 square. |
| Request body | 32 MiB, including the JSON, base64 text, and multipart framing. HTTP headers don't count. [Compression](/api/errors#compression) doesn't raise the limit. |
| All images in the request | 32 MiB, shared by every distinct image after the API processes it. Processing re-encodes each image and can make it larger than the file you sent, so a request of small uploads can still go over. |
| Expanded request | 32 MiB for the text, questions, structure, and images after every reference is replaced by its image. Each use of a reference adds the image again: an image that is 10 MiB after processing, referenced four times, is over the limit. |

All limits include both ends of the range. An image outside them is rejected, never resized to fit. If any image in a request is rejected, the whole request fails: there are no partial answers. See [Errors](#errors) for the status codes.

How many images fit in one request depends on these limits and on the [context length](/models). Images have no separate [rate limits](/api/errors#handling-rate-limits): a request with images counts against the same limits as any other request.

To stay under the request limits, send fewer images, send smaller images, put an image that several questions use in the `state` once instead of in each question's `instructions`, or split the work across requests.

## Preparing images

Send each image as a PNG or JPEG, rotated upright and sized within the [limits](#limits). Prepare each one before you send it:

* **Resize before sending.** Scale the image so its longest side is at most 1568 pixels. A typical 12-megapixel phone photo becomes 1568 × 1176. Scale up, or pad, an image smaller than the minimum.
* **Rotate the pixels upright.** The API removes all metadata (EXIF, color profiles, comments) and does not apply the EXIF orientation. A photo that looks upright in your photo viewer can reach the model sideways, so rotate the pixels themselves first.
* **Send a still image.** For an animation or a video, export the frame you want as a PNG or JPEG. Convert other formats, such as GIF, WebP, or HEIC, to PNG or JPEG.
* **Prefer standard JPEG.** A standard 8-bit baseline JPEG is the safest JPEG to send. Re-save progressive JPEGs as baseline.
* **Re-export a rejected file.** If the API rejects a file that opens fine on your computer, open it in a standard image editor or library and export it again as PNG or JPEG.

This Python example uses the Pillow library to prepare one photo:

```python theme={null}
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

with Image.open("photo.jpg") as original:
    img = ImageOps.exif_transpose(original)  # rotate the pixels upright
    img.thumbnail((1568, 1568))  # longest side at most 1568, same aspect ratio
    # thumbnail only shrinks: upscale or pad an image under the minimum separately
    img.convert("RGB").save("photo-ready.jpg", "JPEG", quality=90)  # baseline JPEG
```

## Image tokens

Each image counts as input tokens, billed at the same per-token [input price](/models) as text. There is no separate charge for images. The `usage.input_tokens` field in the response includes the tokens for every image in the request. Image tokens also count toward the request's [context length](/models).

We'll be providing guidance on estimating image token usage soon.

## Errors

| Status | Cause |
| - | - |
| `400` | Images are not turned on: the request has an image or a Box question but no `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true` header. See [Turning on images](#turning-on-images). |
| `400` | An image or asset was rejected. The file isn't PNG or JPEG, is damaged or incomplete, or is animated; the image is below the minimum width, height, or total pixels; an asset isn't referenced anywhere; the base64 or `format` is invalid; a reference is empty; or the multipart request breaks a [multipart rule](#over-http). |
| `400` | `max_tokens_exceeded`: the images and text together exceed the request's [context length](/models). Send fewer or smaller images, or move images out of `instructions` into the `state`. |
| `413` | The request is over a size limit: an image file, an image's width, height, or total pixels, the request body, all images together, the expanded request, or the reference lengths. See [Limits](#limits). |

If a request has several problems, the error reports one of them. Check the request against [Limits](#limits) and [Preparing images](#preparing-images).


# Introduction
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction

Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first System One model. Send state and typed questions; get structured answers your code can use directly.

Large language models (LLMs) are designed to produce text for humans to read. When you need a model to make a judgment that your code will consume, that creates a mismatch: you are coercing a text-generation system into outputting structured decisions, then parsing the results back into something your code can depend on.

Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first [System One model](/concepts/system-one). System One models are built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly. Jev evaluates typed *questions* against a *state* and returns structured results directly. No text generation, no parsing. You get typed values and probability distributions that your code can branch on, sort by, and route with. Some question types also return [confidence](/confidence), which your code can use to decide whether and how to act on an answer. Each question type's page lists what its answers include.

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 12}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    state["your data<br/>(the state)<br/>text or JSON"]
    questions["your questions<br/>about the data<br/>(several types)"]

    %% not a node - the point where the two lines join into one request
    join@{ shape: f-circ }

    subgraph model["TypeSafe AI model: Jev"]
        evaluate["evaluate each question<br/>against the state<br/>in parallel"]
    end

    state --- join
    questions --- join
    join -- "one request" --> model
    model -- "one response" --> answers["typed answers<br/>+ probabilities<br/>+ confidence<br/>(some types)"]
    answers --> code["<b>your code</b><br/>branch, sort, and route"]

    %% fill:none drops mermaid's own dot; .junction in styles.css redraws
    %% the shape as the three short arms that bridge the join.
    classDef junction fill:none
    class join junction
```

## TypeSafe primitives

TypeSafe exposes *AI primitives*. Similar to software primitives, our AI primitives are modular, composable, structured, reliable, and fast. Each asks a different type of *question* and returns a different type of answer.

| Question type | Goal | Returns |
| - | - | - |
| [Choice](/primitives/choice) | Choose an option from a list | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Score](/primitives/score) | Score the state on a rubric | `score`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Noul](/primitives/noul) | Is this statement true? | `noul` (0–1) |

Any mix of *question* types can go in a single request. Every *question* is evaluated in parallel and in isolation against the same *state* in one go. Adding questions barely changes the response time. Each question is evaluated independently, so adding more questions does not create context-rot.

## Atomic questions, composed in code

System One models work best when each question asks one specific, well-scoped thing. Think of each question as a gut-check determination: the kind of judgment a highly knowledgeable person could make in a few seconds given the right context.

If the question you want to ask would require extended reasoning or weighs multiple independent factors, decompose it. Ask each factor as a separate question, then combine the results with logic in your code. This keeps each individual evaluation reliable and gives you full control over how dimensions are weighted.

For example, instead of "rate this startup pitch," ask separately about market size, technical feasibility, and differentiation. Combine the scores with your own formula. When priorities shift, change a coefficient in your code rather than rewriting a prompt.

## Next steps

* [Quick Start](/introduction/quickstart) — Everything you need to get started immediately.
* [AI Primer](/introduction/machine-learning-primer) — Why TypeSafe trains models for calibrated decisions instead of generated text.
* [Primitives (Questions)](/primitives) — How to define questions, choose a question type, and ask several at once.
* [Confidence](/confidence) — How Jev reports certainty, and how to use it architecturally.
* [Patterns](/patterns) — Common patterns for building systems with TypeSafe.


# Jev with coding agents
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents

What Jev is (and isn't) when you're using a coding agent.

If you found TypeSafe while looking for a model to plug into your coding agent, start here. Jev is **not** a drop-in replacement for the LLM behind Claude Code, Cursor, opencode, Copilot, Muse Spark, Grok Bot, or similar tools. Instead, you can use your coding agent as usual to write code that uses Jev to make decisions.

## Jev is not a chat or code-completion LLM

Jev is a [System One model](/concepts/system-one). It does not generate text, write code, or hold a conversation. It takes a [state](/concepts/state) and a set of typed [questions](/primitives) and returns structured answers your code can use directly:

* A `choice` from a list of options, with per-option probabilities.
* A `score` on a rubric you define.
* A `noul` (0–1) for a true/false statement.

Coding agents rely on an LLM that streams text, calls tools, and edits files based on natural-language instructions. Jev does none of that. There is no `model: "jev-latest"` setting that turns your coding agent into a Jev-powered agent, because the two systems solve different problems.

## What you probably want instead

Pick the row that matches what you were trying to do:

| You wanted to... | Do this |
| - | - |
| Make your coding agent better at *writing code that uses TypeSafe* | Install the [TypeSafe agent skill](/agent-skill). It gives Claude Code, Codex, and other agents full context on the TypeSafe API, the [primitives](/primitives), and the [patterns](/patterns) so they can generate correct TypeSafe integrations for you. |
| Use Jev inside an app or agent you're building — for routing, classification, scoring, guardrails, or any structured decision | Start with the [Quick start](/introduction/quickstart), then read [How to build with TypeSafe](/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) and the [Patterns](/patterns) for common architectures like [routing by probability](/patterns/probability-routing) and [Screen with a Noul first](/patterns/noul-screen). |
| Replace or swap the model that powers a coding agent | Jev isn't the tool for this. Keep using an LLM-based coding agent, and use Jev separately wherever your product needs a fast, calibrated, structured decision. |
| Try Jev before writing any code | Open the [Playground](https://console.typesafe.ai/playground), paste some text as the state, and add a few questions. See the [Quick start](/introduction/quickstart) for a walkthrough. |

## When Jev is worth reaching for

Even though Jev isn't a coding-agent LLM, it's often exactly the right tool *inside* an agent or app you're building with a coding agent. Reach for Jev when your code needs to:

* Route a request to one of a fixed set of destinations, and know how confident that routing is.
* Score something on a rubric (urgency, quality, risk) and branch on the number.
* Check whether a statement is true of a document, message, or record before taking an action.
* Replace a fragile prompt that asks an LLM to "return JSON" with a call that returns typed values by construction.

If any of that matches what you're building, the fastest path in is the [Quick start](/introduction/quickstart), then the [primitives](/primitives) reference for the question types.

## Next steps

* [System One](/concepts/system-one) — What a System One model is and how it differs from an LLM.
* [Quick start](/introduction/quickstart) — Try Jev in the Playground, over HTTP, or with the Python SDK.
* [Agent skill](/agent-skill) — Give your coding agent context on the TypeSafe API.
* [Patterns](/patterns) — Common architectures for building with TypeSafe.


# AI primer
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/machine-learning-primer

Why TypeSafe trains decision models with calibrated probabilities instead of optimizing for generated text.

Most AI products are built around a conversation between a model and a person. TypeSafe starts from a different bet: large-scale automation will be dominated by AI-to-AI and AI-to-software interactions, so the machine interface matters more than the chat interface.

> **We call this Machine Native Intelligence:**
>
> AI with software-like properties such as structure, reliability, observability, testability, speed, consistency, and low cost.

## Building prod, not God

TypeSafe is not trying to build a model that does everything. It is designed for production systems where code needs a narrow decision it can inspect and act on.

Our expectation is that large-scale AI automation will be closer to 99% machine-to-machine interactions and 1% human interaction. That shifts the design target from responses that feel good to read toward outputs that behave predictably inside software.

Read the [TypeSafe manifesto](https://typesafe.ai/manifesto).

## Three post-training approaches

Pretrained language models have been adapted in two major ways. TypeSafe adds a third. RLHF and RLVR are shown here for context; TypeSafe's training path is RLCD.

> [card] RLHF
>
> **Reinforcement learning from human feedback** turned pretrained models into chatbots. It trains models to produce responses people prefer.

> [card] RLVR
>
> **Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards** created reasoning models that are strong at tasks such as mathematics, but slower and more expensive.

> [card] RLCD
>
> **Reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions** trains Jev to return decisions and calibrated probabilities instead of generated text.

RLHF was used to train InstructGPT and ChatGPT and was [co-invented by Diogo Almeida](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=0T4y07QAAAAJ\&hl=en), cofounder of TypeSafe.

![Pretrained language models branch into muted RLHF and RLVR paths and an emphasized RLCD decision-model path.](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/aFVnpmCIX68NpsV1/images/ai-primer/training-paths-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=aFVnpmCIX68NpsV1\&q=85\&s=61898215ac31388d3be15bf583b743ee)

## RLCD and calibrated decisions

RLCD optimizes for a different output contract:

* The model does not generate text.
* It returns decisions and probabilities.
* Higher probability should correspond to a greater chance that the answer is correct.

Calibration makes uncertainty usable by software. Across many predictions from a well-calibrated model:

* Outcomes assigned a probability of `0.2` should occur about 20% of the time.
* Outcomes assigned a probability of `0.8` should occur about 80% of the time.
* Outcomes assigned a probability of `1.0` should occur 100% of the time.

These rates describe groups of predictions, not a guarantee about any single answer. See [Confidence](/confidence) for guidance on deciding when software should act or escalate.

## The problems with RLHF

RLHF teaches a model to say things that people prefer. That objective works well for chatbots, but it can also reward sycophancy and confident-sounding hallucinations.

Preference optimization also causes **mode dropping**: the model learns to favor a particular style, such as instruction following, while reducing the probability of other possible outputs.

![The probability distribution of a base model compared with a narrowed, mode-dropped distribution after RLHF.](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/aFVnpmCIX68NpsV1/images/ai-primer/mode-dropping-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=aFVnpmCIX68NpsV1\&q=85\&s=d51758a6212b526fc243cc9a81572cc7)

> [!WARNING]
>
> An output can be compelling to a person without being reliable enough for unattended automation. Human preference and machine trustworthiness are different optimization targets.

Mode dropping is a milder version of **mode collapse**. In the classic generative-adversarial-network failure mode, a generator learns to produce the same kind of output repeatedly because that output continues to fool the discriminator.

> [accordion] Mode collapse analogy
>
> ![Repeated characters illustrate a GAN suffering from mode collapse.](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/aFVnpmCIX68NpsV1/images/ai-primer/mode-collapse-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=aFVnpmCIX68NpsV1\&q=85\&s=2896f125ad1a5835b31b088fbc64eff1)

RLHF remains a good fit for conversational models. TypeSafe's position is that production automation needs a different training objective—one centered on constrained decisions and calibrated uncertainty.


# Quick start
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart

Get up and running with Jev in 5 minutes.

This guide covers four ways of using Jev, TypeSafe's [System One model](/concepts/system-one), namely: [use our SDK](#code-it-your-first-request), [call our API](#call-it-the-api), [use our agent skill](#vibe-it-the-agent-skill), or [try our browser-based Playground](#try-it-the-playground).

Get an API key from the [TypeSafe console](https://console.typesafe.ai/keys).

## The minimum you should know to use Jev effectively

Each call to Jev sends a request, made of a [state](/concepts/state) (as a simple string or structured object) and a set of [questions](/primitives), and returns one answer per question:

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 12}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    doc["state<br/><i>input text or object<br/>to evaluate</i>"]
    quest["questions<br/><i>what you want to know<br/>about the state</i>"]

    subgraph call["one call to Jev"]
        direction LR
        doc --> api["TypeSafeClient<br/>.system_one()"]
        quest --> api
    end

    api --> ans["answers<br/><i>one result per question</i>"]
```

Jev answers three types of question, called primitives:

| Question type | Goal | Returns |
| - | - | - |
| [Choice](/primitives/choice) | Choose an option from a list | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Score](/primitives/score) | Score the state on a rubric | `score`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Noul](/primitives/noul) | Is this statement true? | `noul` (0–1) |

## Code it: your first request

See how to call Jev from your favourite programming language. The Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript examples use our SDKs; the Bash example calls the API directly.

Create a working directory and set your API key. These setup commands use Bash on macOS, Linux, or Windows with WSL:

```bash wrap theme={null}
mkdir typesafe-quickstart
cd typesafe-quickstart
export TYPESAFE_API_KEY="your-api-key"
```

The example sends a customer support ticket and asks Jev three questions in one request: which team should handle it, how frustrated the customer sounds, and whether the issue is urgent.

> [tab] Python
>
> Requires Python 3.10 or later. Choose a package manager to install the SDK:
>
> > [tab] pip
> >
> > With [pip installed](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/installation/), create a virtual environment and add the SDK:
> >
> > ```bash wrap theme={null}
> > python3 -m venv .venv
> > .venv/bin/pip install typesafe-sdk
> > ```
>
> > [tab] uv
> >
> > With [uv installed](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), initialize a project and add the SDK:
> >
> > ```bash wrap theme={null}
> > uv init --bare
> > uv add typesafe-sdk
> > ```
>
> Save as `route_ticket.py`:
>
> ```python wrap theme={null}
> from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient
>
> ticket = "Our API integration started returning 500 errors on every request about 20 minutes ago, and we can't process any customer orders until this is fixed."
>
> with TypeSafeClient(model="jev-latest") as client:  # Reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
>     response = client.system_one(
>         state=ticket,
>         questions={
>             "department": Choice(
>                 instructions="Which team should handle this",
>                 criteria={
>                     "billing": "Payment or subscription issues",
>                     "technical": "Bugs or integration problems",
>                     "sales": "Pricing or account questions",
>                 },
>             ),
>             "frustration": Score(
>                 instructions="How frustrated the customer appears",
>                 criteria=[
>                     "Calm, just stating facts",
>                     "Frustrated but civil",
>                     "Very angry, strong language",
>                 ],
>             ),
>             "is_urgent": Noul(
>                 instructions="The message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity",
>             ),
>         },
>     )
>
> print(response.choices["department"].choice)
> print(response.scores["frustration"].score)
> print(response.nouls["is_urgent"].noul)
> ```
>
> Run it with either installation method:
>
> ```bash wrap theme={null}
> .venv/bin/python route_ticket.py
> ```

> [tab] JavaScript
>
> Requires Node.js 20 or later. Install the SDK and mark the project as an ES module:
>
> ```bash wrap theme={null}
> npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk
> npm pkg set type=module
> ```
>
> Save as `route_ticket.js`:
>
> ```javascript wrap theme={null}
> import { choice, noul, score, TypeSafeClient } from "@typesafe-ai/sdk";
>
> const ticket = "Our API integration started returning 500 errors on every request about 20 minutes ago, and we can't process any customer orders until this is fixed.";
>
> const client = new TypeSafeClient({ defaultModel: "jev-latest" }); // Reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
> const response = await client.systemOne({
>   state: ticket,
>   questions: {
>     department: choice("Which team should handle this", {
>       billing: "Payment or subscription issues",
>       technical: "Bugs or integration problems",
>       sales: "Pricing or account questions",
>     }),
>     frustration: score("How frustrated the customer appears", [
>       "Calm, just stating facts",
>       "Frustrated but civil",
>       "Very angry, strong language",
>     ]),
>     is_urgent: noul("The message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity"),
>   },
> });
>
> console.log(response.answers.department.choice);
> console.log(response.answers.frustration.score);
> console.log(response.answers.is_urgent.noul);
> ```
>
> Run it:
>

> ```

> [tab] Bash

> set -euo pipefail

>   "model": "jev-latest",
>   "questions": {
>     "department": {
>       "type": "choice",
>       "instructions": "Which team should handle this",
>       "criteria": {
>         "billing": "Payment or subscription issues",
>         "technical": "Bugs or integration problems",
>         "sales": "Pricing or account questions"
>       }
>     },
>     "frustration": {
>       "type": "score",
>       "instructions": "How frustrated the customer appears",
>       "criteria": [
>         "Calm, just stating facts",
>         "Frustrated but civil",
>         "Very angry, strong language"
>       ]
>     },
>     "is_urgent": {
>       "type": "noul",
>       "instructions": "The message conveys urgency or time-sensitivity"
>     }

Jev evaluates each question against the same state and returns answers under the IDs you supplied. `choice` is the team label, `score` is the position on the three-level frustration rubric (0–2), and `noul` is the probability of urgency (0–1).

The Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript examples print those three values:

```text Example output theme={null}
technical
0.67
0.99
```

The Bash example prints the raw JSON response on one line. The Raw Response in the next section shows it formatted, with each answer's confidence and probabilities. These are example results; values can change between Jev releases.

The [client SDKs](/sdk) pages cover installing the Python and JavaScript SDKs, typed answers, and their retry policy.

## Call it: the API

All four code examples in the previous section use this endpoint. The Bash tab above shows the complete HTTP request without an SDK.

```http theme={null}
POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
```
