# Model jaggedness
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness

Jev isn't perfect. Here are some jagged edges we are aware of. Many of these will be fixed in later versions.

Jev is fast, calibrated, and good at common-sense judgment but it is not perfect. It does the best on [System One](/concepts/system-one) tasks. It may struggle with tasks that require additional levels of indirection. It can be quite literal in its understanding. It struggles with tasks that require numeric precision. The [model changelog](/changelog) lists what each Jev release changes.

## The failure modes in detail

| # | Failure mode | Do this instead |
| - | - | - |
| 1 | [Literal reading](#literal-reading) | Write the exact condition, criteria for each available option |
| 2 | [Math and Numbers](#math-and-numbers) | Keep the arithmetic in code |
| 3 | [Date and time comparison](#date-and-time-comparison) | Extract components; compare in code |
| 4 | [Indirection](#indirection) | Reduce hops; point to the relevant state |
| 5 | [Large state full of irrelevant detail](#large-state-full-of-irrelevant-detail) | Filter first; send only what the question needs |
| 6 | [Adversarial content](#adversarial-content) | Write precise prompts, and test edge cases before deploying |
| 7 | [Contradictory instructions and criteria](#contradictory-instructions-and-criteria) | Align the criteria and instruction |
| 8 | [Choice option order](#choice-option-order) | Reorder the options and check the answer is consistent |
| 9 | [Generation](#generation) | Use a generative model |

## Literal reading

Jev answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant. Scoping words, negations, and implied conditions are read at face value. A question will be answered based on the words written in the instruction, whereas a person might have read the intent behind the instructions.

**Instead:** state the exact condition in the `instructions`. Be specific. Put boundary cases in the criteria. When you look at a wrong answer and find yourself explaining what you really meant, that explanation is the missing half of the instruction. Where interpretation is unavoidable, split it into two literal questions and combine them in code.

## Math and Numbers

Jev is not a calculator. We strongly recommend implementing any mathematical logic in code. Jev will perform better on semantic questions than mathematical ones.

### Counting

Jev does not count reliably. This covers characters in a word, occurrences of a term in a passage, and items in a long list. The model recognizes the shape of an answer rather than tallying, and the error grows with the size of the thing being counted.

Before asking a counting question, ask why the count needs a model at all. If the unit is something a regular expression or a parser can find, the count belongs in code and the model has nothing to add.

**Instead:** count in code. When you want to count items matching some criteria, iterate in code over the candidates and ask one question for each, then add up the answers yourself.

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul, TypeSafeClient

client = TypeSafeClient(model="jev-latest")
YES = 0.5  # up to you on what you want the threshold to be, depends on your usecase.

items = ["typesafe", "apple", "california", "banana", "likes", "calibration", "orange", "vertex"]

result = client.system_one(
    {"items": items},
    {
        f"item_{i}": Noul(instructions=f"Is `items[{i}]` the name of a fruit?")
        for i in range(len(items))
    },
)

count = sum(result.nouls[f"item_{i}"].noul > YES for i in range(len(items)))
```

### Numeric representations

Jev will perform better on semantic representations than numeric. For example, questions about colors using hex values will underperform compared to those using the English names. Given RGB triples or hex values it cannot reliably judge whether two values are near each other.

Similarly, questions about high-level programming languages will perform better than questions about low level assembly, or binary encoded instructions.

**Instead:** do the conversion in code and pass in either the computed number or a named bucket. Keep the model for the part that is genuinely a judgment, such as whether a color reads as a warning.

### Math using score

Please do not use score outputs (e.g., expectations and probability) to compute the exact magnitude of a number between two levels of a criterion. You can use the expectation to check if it passes a particular threshold, but Jev's score levels are weak in numerical calibration. It will not be able to help you reconstruct the exact number by interpolating between the nearest two levels.

## Date and time comparison

Jev reads dates as text, not as ordered quantities. Asking which of two dates comes first, how far apart they are, or whether one falls inside a window is unreliable. It gets worse with mixed formats, relative references and domain boundaries such as quarters, settlement windows, and accrual periods.

**Instead:** split the work. Extraction is a judgment, so give it to the model. Arithmetic is not, so keep it in code.

Every part of a date is a small closed set: twelve months, thirty-one possible days, a bounded range of years. That turns extraction into a [Choice](/primitives/choice) over enumerated options rather than free-form parsing, and it gives you somewhere to put an explicit "not stated" option so a missing part is reported rather than guessed. Code assembles the parts into a real date and owns everything after that, including ordering, duration, offset, and weekday.

The [date extraction cookbook](/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook) has the worked version, including relative dates and sending low-confidence dates to a person.

## Indirection

Instructions carrying double negatives or complex indirection are answered less reliably. A question about a property of a property or something that requires multiple hops of reasoning costs accuracy.

**Instead:** write your instructions as directly as possible. When possible, identify the relevant parts of state by name.

## Large state full of irrelevant detail

Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision. Unrelated detail acts as a distractor, and a large state makes it harder to tell which part of the input produced a wrong answer.

**Instead:** retrieve and filter in code first, and send only the fields the question needs. When it's not possible to filter in state, you can use a [Noul](/primitives/noul) to filter for relevance. The [classifying RAG passages cookbook](/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages) has a worked example.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Context length limit.** The `state` counts once against each of Jev's context limits, the [per-request context and the per-question context](/models#context-length).

## Adversarial content

State is data, and Jev does not treat it as hostile by default. Content written to adversarially steer the model, whether that is an injected instruction, a deliberately misleading framing, or text that argues for its own classification, can move the answer. We expect to improve on this in the future.

**Instead:** be explicit in the criteria. Test your integration thoroughly before deploying it to many users.

## Contradictory instructions and criteria

When the `instructions` and the `criteria` ask for different things, Jev might get confused. The best performance comes from clear phrasing. For example, a Noul where `true` maps to no and `false` maps to yes will perform worse. Aim for instructions which are easy for the average person to read and understand.

**Instead:** treat the criteria as an extension of the instruction. Align the two using clear and precise language.

## Choice option order

In some cases, we observed that the order of a [Choice](/primitives/choice)'s options can affect the answer, and Jev leans toward the option that comes first.

**Instead:** reorder the options to double check that the answer stays consistent.

## Generation

Jev is not trained to generate text. While you can force it to by chaining choices, this will not work well and will be very slow. For data extraction, it is better to extract possible options using regex or a generative model and let Jev pick the correct extraction.

**Instead:** when the answer space is bounded, turn extraction into a [Choice](/primitives/choice) over the options rather than asking for the value itself. If you really need to generate text... there are other models for that.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **As a reminder, avoid the following:**
>
> * Asking the model something code can compute exactly.
> * Hiding several judgments inside one question.
> * System Two tasks: more layers of indirections
> * Giving it more context in `state` than the question needs. Jev suffers from context rot, so unrelated material in the `state` costs you accuracy.

> [!TIP]
>
> Found a failure mode that belongs on this list? We want to hear about it. Reach us on [Discord](https://discord.gg/typesafe).


# Models
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/models

Jev is TypeSafe's flagship model and the first [System One model](/concepts/system-one). Every model on this page is served by the same endpoint, `POST /v1/systemone`. The request's `model` field selects which one handles it; see the [API reference](/api) for the full request shape.

## Current models

| | Jev 1.14 | Jev 1.13 |
| :- | :- | :- |
| Model ID | `jev-1.14.0` | `jev-1.13.0` |
| Price (per Btok / per Mtok) | \$42 / \$0.042 | \$42 / \$0.042 |
| Context length | 64k per-request / 32k per-question | 64k per-request / 32k per-question |
| Input | Text | Text |

Jev 1.14 is the newest Jev release, available from October 14, 2026.

* **Price:** You pay per input token. Output tokens are free. A Btok is a billion tokens and an Mtok is a million tokens.
* **Context length:** Two limits, the per-request context and the per-question context. See [Context length](#context-length). To raise both, see [Long context](#long-context).
* **Input:** Jev reads natural-language text, sent as a string, a JSON object, or an array of text values. It does not accept audio or video. Convert those into text or structured fields before you send them as `state`. See [State](/concepts/state) for the shapes `state` accepts.

## Context length

Jev ingests the `state` once and evaluates every question against it in parallel. A request has to fit two context limits:

* **Per-request context** (`per_request_context`): the `state` plus all questions combined.
* **Per-question context** (`per_question_context`): the `state` plus any one question.

There is no separate limit on the number of questions in a request. Any number of questions is allowed as long as the request fits both limits. See [Speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out) for packing many questions into one request, and [Model jaggedness](/model-jaggedness) for how accuracy shifts as the state grows.

To raise both limits, see [Long context](#long-context).

### Long context

Long context is off by default and works on both Jev 1.14 and Jev 1.13. To turn it on, send the `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true` header with each request that needs it. With the header, the per-request context and the per-question context are both 262k tokens. Requests without the header keep the default limits in the table above.

```bash theme={null}
curl https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true" \
  -d '{
    "model": "jev-latest",
    "state": "<a long contract, transcript, or record>",
    "questions": {
      "has_termination_clause": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Does the `state` include a clause that lets either party end the agreement early?"
      }
    }
  }'
```

Long context costs the same per token as any other request. It is slower and less accurate than staying within the default limits, so turn it on only for requests that need it.

## Rate limits

Rate limits are set per organization. Your organization's current limits are in the [developer console](https://console.typesafe.ai/rate-limits).

Limits are measured in tokens per second and requests per second. A request over either limit returns `429 Too Many Requests`. Our [client SDKs](/sdk) retry these requests by default, waiting longer between each attempt, and follow the `retry-after` header when the response includes one. If you call the HTTP API directly, see [Handling rate limits](/api/errors#handling-rate-limits).

Higher limits are available on custom and enterprise plans. To request a higher limit, fill out the [rate limit increase request form](https://support.typesafe.ai/forms/rate-limit-increase-request).

## Aliases

An alias is a model name that points to a versioned model ID. Send it in the `model` field the same way you send a model ID.

| Alias | Points to | Meaning |
| :- | :- | :- |
| `jev-latest` | `jev-1.14.0` | The most recent stable, official release. The default in our client SDKs, and the name the examples in these docs use. |
| `jev-preview` | `jev-1.14.0` | The most recent release, official or not. Moves ahead of `jev-latest` when a preview build is available. |

> [!WARNING]
>
> `jev-preview` currently points to the same model as `jev-latest`. There is no preview build available right now.

An alias moves when a new release ships, so its answers can change without any change to your code. Each response's `model` field gives the versioned ID that answered, so you can log which model produced each result. If you have tuned confidence thresholds against one version, send that version's ID instead of the alias, and switch to the new version when you are ready.

## Customizing Jev

Jev is not fine-tuned or LoRA-adapted with customer data. It is trained with [RLCD](/introduction/machine-learning-primer) to return calibrated decisions, and the same weights serve every account. You shape its answers to your domain through the request rather than through per-account weights:

* Put your proprietary content, records, and reference material in the `state` field. See [State](/concepts/state).
* Encode your domain rules and boundary cases in the `instructions` and `criteria` of each question. See [How to build with TypeSafe](/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) and [Advanced: structure](/primitives/advanced).
* Decompose broad judgments into atomic questions and combine the outputs in code. See [Composite scoring](/patterns/composite-scoring) and the [AutoResearch cookbook](/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery) for training a downstream classical model on Jev's probabilities.

## Language support

Jev accepts natural-language text. English is the primary training language and where accuracy is currently best. Other languages, including CJK scripts, are handled but not equally well; test on your own content before relying on Jev for a non-English workload, and pay close attention to [Confidence](/confidence) when routing.

## Data handling

Jev is not trained on customer requests or responses. See [Legal](/legal) for the Data Processing Agreement, the Privacy Policy, and details on zero data retention (ZDR) for enterprise customers.

## Listing models

`GET /v1/models` returns the names your account can send in the `model` field, each with a description and a release date. It currently lists the aliases. Versioned IDs such as `jev-1.14.0` are accepted by the `model` field whether or not they appear in the list.

```bash cURL theme={null}
curl https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/models \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY"
```

```python Python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import TypeSafeClient

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    for model in client.models.list().models:
        print(model.name, model.release_date, model.description)
```

```typescript JavaScript theme={null}
import { TypeSafeClient } from "@typesafe-ai/sdk";

const client = new TypeSafeClient();
const models = await client.models.list();
for (const model of models) {
  console.log(model.name, model.release_date, model.description);
}
```

**models** `array` *required*

One entry per model or alias.

**properties**

**name** `string` *required*

The model ID or alias, as accepted by the `model` field.

**description** `string` *required*

What the model is for.

**release\_date** `string` *required*

When the model or alias was released.

See the [Python](/sdk/python/api/clients/sync#typesafe_sdk.Models.list) and [JavaScript](/sdk/javascript/api/interfaces/Models) SDK references for the full method signatures.


# Patterns
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns

Architectural patterns for building systems with TypeSafe.

TypeSafe is designed to sit within a larger system, powering decisions with AI. Learning to think in terms of discrete, atomic decisions that compose into complex system behavior is a key skill for getting the most out of TypeSafe.

This section assumes you know the [TypeSafe primitives](/primitives) and understand [how confidence works](/confidence). If not, read those first.

## The patterns

| Pattern | What it does | Benefits |
| - | - | - |
| [Speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out) | Send many questions in a single request, including speculative ones, and let your code decide what's relevant | Cost, Speed |
| [Screen with a Noul first](/patterns/noul-screen) | Ask one cheap yes/no question first, and run the expensive stage only when it passes | Cost, Speed |
| [Companion Noul](/patterns/companion-noul) | Pair a Choice question with a Noul question that asks whether anything fits, so your code can tell when nothing does | Reliability |
| [Routing by confidence](/patterns/confidence-routing) | Send a Score answer to a person when its confidence is low, and route the rest on the score | Reliability, Safety |
| [Routing by probability](/patterns/probability-routing) | Set a higher probability threshold for riskier actions | Reliability, Safety |
| [Composite scoring](/patterns/composite-scoring) | Combine several dimensions of analysis into a single score | Cost, Reliability, Speed |

## Patterns by goal

Every pattern splits a decision into small System One questions and leaves the decision to your code: Jev answers each question with a probability, and your code decides what happens next. Pick by what you need:

* **Spend less.** [Speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out) asks everything in one request. [Screen with a Noul first](/patterns/noul-screen) keeps the expensive stages from running on inputs that don't need them.
* **Act safely.** [Routing by probability](/patterns/probability-routing) sets a higher threshold for riskier actions. [Routing by confidence](/patterns/confidence-routing) sends a Score answer that is spread across the scale to a person. [Companion Noul](/patterns/companion-noul) catches the case where nothing fits.
* **Combine answers.** [Composite scoring](/patterns/composite-scoring) adds up several Scores with weights you control.

> [!TIP]
>
> We're always keen to learn how people are making use of our primitives. If you've found a killer use case you think should be mentioned here, feel free to drop us a note!


# Companion Noul
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/companion-noul

Pair a Choice with a Noul that asks whether any option fits, so your code can tell when none does.

A Choice question always picks an option, even when none of them applies. Ask which of three things an input is about, and an input about none of them still gets an answer, possibly with a high probability. The model is answering the question it was asked, so it picks whichever of the three options is closest.

To fix this, add a second question to the same request: a Noul question that asks whether any of the options fits at all. Your code uses the answer to the Choice only when the Noul is a clear yes.

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    message["support message<br/>+ product list"]

    subgraph req["Jev evaluates questions<br/>in parallel"]
        direction TB
        product["<b>Choice:</b> which product?"]
        any["<b>Noul:</b> is message about<br/>one of our products?"]
        %% Invisible links stack the questions; they are answered in parallel.
        product ~~~ any
    end

    message -- "one request<br/>message + 2 questions" --> req
    req -- "one response<br/>2 answers" --> check{"<b>Noul above 0.7?</b><br/>your code"}
    check green_yes@-- "yes, and the Choice<br/>is above 0.7" --> team["product team queue"]
    check blue_mid@-- "between 0.3 and 0.7,<br/>or the Choice is unsure" --> agent["general support agent"]
    check purple_no@-- "below 0.3: ignore the Choice" --> general["general inbox"]
    %% Branch colours (styles.css): node classes and green_/blue_/purple_ edge ids.
    class team neonGreen
    class agent neonBlue
    class general neonPurple
    %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
    green_yes@{ animate: true }
    blue_mid@{ animate: true }
    purple_no@{ animate: true }
```

## Example: routing messages to product teams

Say you sell three products, and you send each support message to the relevant product team. Messages about anything else, such as a lamp from another shop or a note from a recruiter, go to a general inbox instead.

### Ask which product, and whether any fits

Both questions refer to the product list by its key in the state, `products`. Jev sees the Choice question's option names, so names such as `desk_pro` say what each product is. The `false` criterion on the Noul question lists what counts as a no: another product, a service, or something you don't sell.

Try it in the Playground →

Jev's response:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.14.0",
  "answers": {
    "product": {
      "type": "choice",
      "choice": "desk_pro",
      "confidence": 0.94,
      "probabilities": {
        "desk_pro": 0.96,
        "chair_lite": 0.01,
        "monitor_arm": 0.03
      }
    },
    "about_our_product": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.02
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 549,
    "output_tokens": 63
  }
}
```

The Choice picks `desk_pro` at 0.96, with a confidence of 0.94. Nothing in that answer tells you the message isn't about your desk. Of the three options, a desk lamp is closest to a desk. The companion Noul reads 0.02, which says the message isn't about any of your products. Here are Jev's answers for four different messages:

| Message | Choice | Top probability | Noul |
| - | - | - | - |
| "The motor on my standing desk has started making a grinding noise... the 140 cm one" | `desk_pro` | 1.00 | 0.98 |
| "The chair arrived but the monitor arm didn't. Can you check where the arm is?" | `monitor_arm` | 1.00 | 0.99 |
| "My desk lamp stopped working after two weeks..." | `desk_pro` | 0.96 | 0.02 |
| "I'm a recruiter working with several furniture retailers and wondered if your head of operations is open to a quick call" | `desk_pro` | 0.81 | 0.02 |

### Trust the Choice only when a product fits

Read the Noul first. On a clear no, ignore the Choice and send the message to the general inbox. A clear yes says the message is about one of your products, but not which one, so also check the probability of the product the Choice picked. If both are high, send the message straight to that product team. Otherwise, a general support agent decides, with the Choice's pick passed along as a suggestion.

```python title="route.py" theme={null}
YES = 0.7
NO = 0.3
PRODUCT_SURE = 0.7


def route(message_id, response):
    about_ours = response.answers["about_our_product"].noul
    product = response.answers["product"]
    product_probability = product.probabilities[product.choice]

    if about_ours < NO:
        # Nothing fits. The Choice's answer is noise; don't read it.
        send_to_general_inbox(message_id)

    elif about_ours > YES and product_probability > PRODUCT_SURE:
        # The Choice is answering a question that applies, and it clearly picked one product. Use it.
        send_to_product_team(message_id, product.choice)

    else:
        # Unsettled, or about our products but not clearly which one:
        # a person decides, with the Choice's top option as a hint.
        send_to_general_agent(message_id, suggested_product=product.choice)
```

## Why an `other` option falls short

Adding `other: 'Something else'` to the Choice question looks like less work, and it used to be the usual advice. But `other` competes with the product options for probability. A message that is partly about a product and partly about something else splits its probability between `other` and that product, and neither number tells your code what to do. With a companion Noul, the Choice question only picks among the products, and a separate question with concrete `true` and `false` criteria decides whether any product fits. In our tests, that usually works better.

> [!NOTE]
>
> [Box](/primitives/box), which is a question type for finding where something is in an image, has the same problem: it always returns a location in an image. Pair it with a Noul question such as "Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?" so your code knows whether the box marks a mug at all.

## Other ways to use a companion Noul

* **One Noul question per option.** When a message can be about more than one product, a Choice has to split its probability between them. Ask one Noul question per product instead, and read each one on its own. Then the case where nothing fits needs no extra question, because every Noul comes back low.
* **As a screen.** Ask a Noul question first, and run the expensive step, which may require a Choice or Score, only when the answer is a clear yes. See [screen with a Noul first](/patterns/noul-screen).
* **Candidates from code.** The options don't have to be a fixed list. Your code can pull possible values out of the text and use them as the options in the Choice question, and the companion Noul question asks whether the right value is among them. The [value extraction cookbook](/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook) builds candidates in code this way, but it uses a `none` option instead of a companion Noul.


# Composite scoring
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring

Break a complex judgment into atomic scores, combine with weights you control in code.

Oftentimes we want to rank a set of items based on several criteria at once. Composite scoring is an easy way to think about this: break the judgment into independent dimensions, score each one separately, and combine them with weights you control in code.

## Example: screening resumes

Let's imagine you are processing resumes for engineering roles. You want to rank the candidates based on several criteria, and ultimately select the top X candidates for further review.

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    resume["candidate resume"]

    subgraph req["Jev evaluates questions<br/>in parallel"]
        direction TB
        py["<b>Score:</b> Python depth"]
        lead["<b>Score:</b> team leadership"]
        arch["<b>Score:</b> system design"]
        general["<b>Score:</b> generalist"]
        %% Invisible links stack the questions; they are answered in parallel.
        py ~~~ lead ~~~ arch ~~~ general
    end

    resume -- "one request<br/>resume + 4 questions" --> req
    req -- "one response<br/>4 score answers" --> normalize["<b>normalize scores to 0–1</b><br/>divide each by 4 in your code"]
    normalize ic_weights@--> ic["<b>senior IC weights</b><br/>40% Python + 10% leadership<br/>40% design + 10% generalist"]
    normalize em_weights@--> em["<b>engineering manager weights</b><br/>15% Python + 40% leadership<br/>20% design + 25% generalist"]
    ic --> rank["rank candidates<br/>for each role"]
    em --> rank
    %% The two weighting paths flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
    ic_weights@{ animate: true }
    em_weights@{ animate: true }
```

### Score each dimension separately

Send the resume with one Score question per dimension. Each question asks for a single judgment, so each score can be weighted on its own later.

Try it in the Playground →

### Combine the scores with weights

Each dimension is normalized to 0–1 and weighted. The weights give you an easy way to adjust the relative importance of each dimension, without losing any of the nuance of the individual scores.

```python title="scoring.py" theme={null}
py      = response.answers["python_depth"].score / 4
lead    = response.answers["team_leadership"].score / 4
arch    = response.answers["system_design"].score / 4
general = response.answers["generalist"].score / 4

# Senior IC
ic_score = (0.40 * py) + (0.10 * lead) + (0.40 * arch) + (0.10 * general)

# Engineering Manager
em_score = (0.15 * py) + (0.40 * lead) + (0.20 * arch) + (0.25 * general)
```

This gives you the ability to rank the candidates based on the composite score. But more importantly, it gives you visibility into how exactly the final score is being calculated. If the highest ranking candidates are not matching your expectations, you can adjust the weights to find the right balance.


# Routing by confidence
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/confidence-routing

Use confidence as a second axis. The score tells you what; confidence tells you whether to act on it.

A Score answer gives you a position on the scale, `score`, and a [confidence](/confidence) from 0 to 1 that says how certain the answer is. Check the confidence first: send an answer whose probability is spread across the scale to a person, and route the rest on the score.

## Example: triaging bug reports

Let's imagine you are building a bug tracker that triages incoming reports. A cosmetic issue can wait in the backlog, a broken feature goes into the current sprint, and anything that stops users completing a core task goes straight to the on-call engineer. A report that doesn't make its severity clear should go to a person before anyone messages the engineer.

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    report["bug report"]

    subgraph req["Jev evaluates<br/>the question"]
        severity["<b>Score:</b> severity"]
    end

    report -- "one request<br/>report + severity<br/>question" --> req
    req -- "one response<br/>severity score +<br/>confidence" --> check{"<b>confidence<br/>at least 0.5?</b><br/>your code"}
    check blue_triage@-- "no" --> triage["a person triages<br/>the report"]
    check -- "yes" --> level{"<b>how severe?</b><br/>severity.score"}
    level green_backlog@-- "below 1.5" --> backlog["add to the backlog"]
    level green_sprint@-- "1.5 to<br/>under 2.5" --> sprint["add to this sprint"]
    level green_page@-- "2.5 or more" --> page["message the on-call<br/>engineer"]
    %% Branch colours (styles.css): node classes and green_/blue_/purple_/orange_ edge ids.
    class backlog,sprint,page neonGreen
    class triage neonBlue
    %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
    blue_triage@{ animate: true }
    green_backlog@{ animate: true }
    green_sprint@{ animate: true }
    green_page@{ animate: true }
```

### Score how severe the report is

Send the report with one Score question. Its five levels run from a cosmetic issue to a critical one.

Try it in the Playground →

Jev's answer doesn't say whether the update lost the notes or the user deleted them:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.14.0",
  "answers": {
    "severity": {
      "type": "score",
      "score": 3.19,
      "confidence": 0.34,
      "legend": {
        "0": "Cosmetic: wording, layout, or styling only",
        "1": "Minor: something misbehaves, but users can still do what they wanted",
        "2": "Major with a workaround: a feature is broken, but there is another way to get the job done",
        "3": "Major with no workaround: users cannot complete a core task",
        "4": "Critical: data loss, a security hole, or the product is down for everyone"
      },
      "probabilities": {
        "0": 0.01,
        "1": 0.14,
        "2": 0.07,
        "3": 0.19,
        "4": 0.59
      }
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 435,
    "output_tokens": 17
  }
}
```

A score of 3.19 on its own would message the on-call engineer. The probabilities tell a different story: most of the probability is on "critical", in case the update lost the notes, but 0.14 is on "minor", in case the user deleted them. The probability spread brings the confidence down to 0.34.

### Send unsettled scores to a person, route the rest

Check confidence before reading the score, and route on the score only when the check passes.

```python theme={null}
severity = response.answers["severity"]

if severity.confidence < 0.5:
    # The probability is spread across the scale. A person reads the report first.
    send_to_triage(report_id)

elif severity.score < 1.5:
    add_to_backlog(report_id)

elif severity.score < 2.5:
    add_to_sprint(report_id)

else:
    message_on_call(report_id)
```

The "Notes gone?" report goes to triage, where a person can ask the reporter whether the notes were deleted. Reports with a clear severity route straight through, as these recorded `jev-1.14.0` answers show:

| Report | `score` | `confidence` | Outcome |
| - | - | - | - |
| Typo on the settings page | 0.0 | 1.0 | backlog |
| PDF export fails over 50 pages; splitting the document works | 2.0 | 1.0 | this sprint |
| Checkout returns a 500 error for every customer | 3.36 | 0.7 | message on-call |
| Notes gone after the update, or maybe deleted | 3.19 | 0.34 | triage |

## When two levels split the answer

For a Score, if two levels have the highest and equal probabilities, the score is much higher if those two levels are next to each other than if they are not. The further they are apart, the lower the score.
A Score's confidence counts probability on a neighboring level as only a small spread. That can be an issue if you set a threshold between those two levels: an answer split between them can pass a confidence check and land on the wrong side of the threshold. The [Score explorer](/confidence#score) shows how the distance between levels changes confidence.

When a decision depends on which side of a level boundary the answer falls, add up the probabilities of the levels on the side that matters:

```python theme={null}
blocked = severity.probabilities[3] + severity.probabilities[4]

if blocked >= 0.3:
    # A real chance users are blocked. Message someone rather than wait for the sprint.
    message_on_call(report_id)
```

[Routing by probability](/patterns/probability-routing) builds a whole router on probabilities like this, with a separate threshold for each action.


# Speculative fan-out
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out

Send many questions in a single request, including speculative ones, and let your code decide what's relevant.

Because Jev answers many questions in a single API call, we recommend putting all of the questions your system needs in a single request, and then using code to decide what is relevant after the fact. All questions are evaluated in parallel, so adding more questions usually has little effect on response time.

## Example: triaging support tickets

Let's imagine you are building a support system that needs to triage support tickets. You need to classify the ticket into a category. If it's a bug report, you also need to determine the severity of the bug.

Instead of asking for the category first and then the severity in a follow-up call, you can ask for both at the same time. If the ticket is not a bug report, you simply ignore the results of the bug severity question.

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 8, "bottom": 60}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    t["support ticket"]

    subgraph req["Jev evaluates each question<br/>against the ticket in parallel"]
        direction TB
        c["<b>Choice:</b> category"]
        b["<b>Score:</b> bug severity"]
        r["<b>Noul:</b> reproducible steps?"]
        f["<b>Noul:</b> refund requested?"]
        s["<b>Score:</b> frustration"]
        %% invisible links: without an edge these share a rank and sit side by side
        c ~~~ b ~~~ r ~~~ f ~~~ s
    end

    t -- "one request<br/>ticket + 5 questions" --> req
    req -- "one response: 5 answers<br/>decisions + probabilities" --> route{"<b>filter, combine, and route</b><br/>in your code"}
    route blue_bug@-- "bug_report" --> eng["read severity + repro steps<br/>escalate or backlog"]
    route orange_bill@-- "billing" --> bill["refund requested<br/>send to billing"]
    route purple_feat@-- "feature_request" --> feat["log it<br/>sent to devs"]
    %% Branch colours (styles.css): node classes and green_/blue_/purple_/orange_ edge ids.
    class eng neonBlue
    class bill neonOrange
    class feat neonPurple
    %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
    blue_bug@{ animate: true }
    orange_bill@{ animate: true }
    purple_feat@{ animate: true }
```

### Ask every question in one request

Send the ticket with every question your code might need: the category, plus questions that only matter for some categories.

Try it in the Playground →

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Speculative questions:** `bug_severity` and `has_reproducible_steps` only matter if the ticket is a bug report. `refund_requested` only matters for billing. We include all upfront because additional questions usually have little effect on response time. If the ticket turns out to be a feature request, the bug severity result will be irrelevant, in which case your code path simply ignores it.

### Route in your code

Your code decides what is relevant based on the classification result:

```python title="triage.py" theme={null}
category = response.answers["category"]
bug_severity = response.answers["bug_severity"]
bug_repro = response.answers["has_reproducible_steps"]
refund = response.answers["refund_requested"]
frustration = response.answers["frustration"]

if category.choice == "bug_report":
    if bug_severity.score > 1.5 and bug_repro.noul > 0.6:
        escalate_to_engineering(ticket_id, severity="high")
    else:
        add_to_bug_backlog(ticket_id)

elif category.choice == "billing":
    if refund.noul > 0.7:
        route_to_billing_with_flag(ticket_id, refund_likely=True)
    else:
        route_to_billing(ticket_id)

elif category.choice == "feature_request":
    log_feature_request(ticket_id)

# Frustration is useful regardless of category
if frustration.score > 1.5:
    flag_for_priority_response(ticket_id)
```

Everything needed for the full decision tree comes from one call. Speculative questions are ignored when irrelevant and save a round trip when they are not.


# Screen with a Noul first
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/noul-screen

Ask one yes/no question first, and run the expensive step only when the answer is a clear yes.

Not every input needs your expensive step. Ask one Noul question first, with a small state such as the input on its own, and run the expensive step only when the answer is a clear yes. A clear no gets cheaper handling, and an answer it can't settle gets a rule of its own, so every input ends up handled.

![An inbox of messages flows toward one Noul question. Each message is held while the question is answered, then takes one of three exits: a clear no is filed away, an unsettled answer is set aside for a quick look, and a clear yes continues into the full triage request with its customer record attached.](https://mintcdn.com/ts-docs/0mdJYbuyjcLi9rbO/patterns/noul-screen-hero-light.gif?s=156a517da1ccc828140f49adf6c59fcd)

## When to screen first

Jev answers all the questions in a request in parallel and reads the state once, so you pay for the state once. If the later questions would use the same state, don't split them off: send them all in one request and let your code ignore the answers that don't apply, we call this pattern [speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out). Asking first is worth the extra request when the later step costs something the first question doesn't:

* **A bigger state.** The next step needs the customer record, the full thread, or an attachment that code has to fetch first.
* **A slower model.** The next step is an LLM call.
* **A person.** The next step needs someone to look at the item.

## Example: triaging a shared inbox

Say you're building a shared-inbox tool. Everything arrives in one stream: customers asking about orders, newsletters, payment receipts, thank-you notes, and the occasional "just so you know". Full triage means fetching the sender's account and order history, then asking several questions about the message. A Noul question that sees only the message, as it arrived, can decide which messages get full triage.

### Ask whether the sender expects a reply

We ask one thing the message alone can settle: is the sender waiting for a reply? Instead of saying "not waiting", the `false` criterion lists the kinds of message with nothing to answer, including a note from a person that needs no reply.

Try it in the Playground →

Tom's message reports a problem but asks for nothing: the desk is already built, and the message doesn't say whether Tom wants to hear back. The answer is neither a clear yes nor a clear no:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.14.0",
  "answers": {
    "expects_reply": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.44
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 414,
    "output_tokens": 21
  }
}
```

Jev's answers to the same question for five different messages:

| Message | `expects_reply` |
| - | - |
| "I ordered a standing desk two weeks ago and the tracking hasn't updated... I'm moving on the 30th and need it before then." | 0.98 |
| "Just so you know, the desk arrived with one of the cross-bar screws missing. I had a spare so it's built now." | 0.44 |
| "Thanks, the desk arrived yesterday and it's great." | 0.10 |
| "20% off every desk and chair until Sunday. Unsubscribe \| View in browser" | 0.02 |
| "Your payment of \$129.00 was successful... replies to this address are not monitored." | 0.02 |

### Handle yes, no and unsure

Compare the Noul with two thresholds: above 0.7 counts as yes, and below 0.3 counts as no. Both are good starting points. An answer between them means the message doesn't settle the question, so give it its own outcome instead of rounding it to yes or no.

```python title="screen.py" theme={null}
YES_ABOVE = 0.7
NO_BELOW = 0.3


def handle(message_id, screen_response):
    expects_reply = screen_response.answers["expects_reply"].noul

    if expects_reply < NO_BELOW:
        # Newsletters, receipts, notifications. Nothing to answer.
        file_away(message_id)

    elif expects_reply > YES_ABOVE:
        # A person is waiting. Fetch what triage needs and run the full request.
        customer = fetch_customer(message_id)
        triage(message_id, customer)

    else:
        # Something to look at, but maybe nothing to answer. One glance settles it.
        queue_for_quick_look(message_id)
```

Of the five messages above, one leads to a triage request: the standing desk that hasn't arrived. The thank-you note and the two automated messages are filed away, and the missing-screw note goes to a person for a quick look.

### Triage only the messages that need a reply

Fetch the customer record only for messages with a clear yes. The triage request sends the record with the message and asks questions that each check one thing: `repeat_contact` reads `customer.previous_contacts`, and `urgency` counts from `message.received`. A real triage stage would ask more questions than this.

Try it in the Playground →

Jev's response:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.14.0",
  "answers": {
    "request": {
      "type": "choice",
      "choice": "order_status",
      "confidence": 1.0,
      "probabilities": {
        "order_status": 1.0,
        "return_or_refund": 0.0,
        "product_question": 0.0,
        "complaint": 0.0
      }
    },
    "urgency": {
      "type": "score",
      "score": 1.99,
      "confidence": 0.98,
      "legend": {
        "0": "No deadline is mentioned",
        "1": "The sender wants an answer soon but gives no date",
        "2": "The sender names a date or event within a week"
      },
      "probabilities": {
        "0": 0.0,
        "1": 0.01,
        "2": 0.99
      }
    },
    "repeat_contact": {
      "type": "noul",
      "noul": 0.99
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 803,
    "output_tokens": 84
  }
}
```

The `repeat_contact` answer comes from the record: with no previous contacts on file, the same message got 0.05.

From here, your routing code acts on the answers. Dana's urgent, repeated order-status request could go to the front of the queue.

## Other ways to screen

* **Check a cheap step first.** Run the cheap step, ask a Noul whether its output is right, and send only the outputs that fail that check to the expensive model.
* **Several screens.** A content pipeline might check first for "written in English" and then for "about our product". Each check removes inputs before the next, more expensive step.


# Routing by probability
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/probability-routing

Give riskier actions a higher probability threshold. The answer says what to do, and its probability says whether to do it.

Every Jev answer comes with [probabilities](/confidence). For each action your code can take, decide how high the probability must be before you take it. Riskier actions get higher thresholds, and an answer below the threshold gets its own outcome, such as asking the user to clarify, instead of counting as a yes. The actions can be anything your code can call: a function in your app, an LLM, or a person.

## Example: acting on voice banking commands

Say you're building a voice banking interface where users manage their account by speaking. Before acting on a command, you want to be reasonably sure what the user asked for, and very sure for the riskier actions.

```mermaid actions={true} theme={null}
%%{init: {"fontFamily": "Inter, sans-serif", "flowchart": {"rankSpacing": 35, "wrappingWidth": 300, "subGraphTitleMargin": {"top": 12, "bottom": 36}}}}%%
flowchart LR
    command["voice banking command"]

    subgraph req["Jev evaluates<br/>the question"]
        intent["<b>Choice:</b> intent"]
    end

    command -- "one request<br/>command + intent<br/>question" --> req
    req -- "one response<br/>intent answer +<br/>probabilities" --> check{"<b>probability high enough?</b><br/>your code"}
    check red_low@-- "below 0.7<br/>or other intent" --> human["send to a support agent"]
    check orange_balance@-- "check_balance<br/>at least 0.7" --> balance["show the balance"]
    check yellow_confirm@-- "approve_transfer<br/>0.7 to 0.9" --> confirm["clarify the request"]
    check green_approve@-- "approve_transfer<br/>above 0.9" --> approve["show transfer details<br/>and require confirmation"]
    %% Branch colours (styles.css): a confidence gradient, red -> orange -> yellow -> green.
    class human neonRed
    class balance neonOrange
    class confirm neonYellow
    class approve neonGreen
    %% Branch edges flow (styles.css pauses this under prefers-reduced-motion).
    red_low@{ animate: true }
    orange_balance@{ animate: true }
    yellow_confirm@{ animate: true }
    green_approve@{ animate: true }
```

### Ask what the user wants to do

Send the user's command with one Choice question. The `other` option catches commands this system doesn't handle. It keeps the example short, but a [companion Noul](/patterns/companion-noul#why-an-other-option-falls-short) usually works better as a catch-all.

Try it in the Playground →

Jev's response:

```json theme={null}
{
  "model": "jev-1.14.0",
  "answers": {
    "intent": {
      "type": "choice",
      "choice": "check_balance",
      "confidence": 1.0,
      "probabilities": {
        "check_balance": 1.0,
        "approve_transfer": 0.0,
        "other": 0.0
      }
    }
  },
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 343,
    "output_tokens": 41
  }
}
```

### Set a threshold for each action

Compare the probability of the chosen option, `probabilities[choice]`, against the threshold. That number is how likely it is that this option is what the user asked for.

```python theme={null}
action = response.answers["intent"]
likelihood = action.probabilities[action.choice]

# Below 0.7 on any action, the command didn't settle the intent. Route to a human.
if likelihood < 0.7:
    route_to_support_agent(account_id)

elif action.choice == "check_balance":
    # Low stakes. 0.7 is sufficient.
    show_balance(account_id)

elif action.choice == "approve_transfer":
    if likelihood > 0.9:
        # Identifying the intent starts confirmation; it does not approve a transfer.
        show_transfer_for_confirmation(account_id)
    else:
        # Clarify what the user wants before opening the transfer workflow.
        ask_user_to_clarify("Would you like to review the pending transfer?")

else:
    route_to_support_agent(account_id)
```

The thresholds only choose which workflow runs; none of them moves money. A clear transfer request opens a confirmation screen with the amount and recipient, and the transfer runs only after the user confirms them. A less certain one asks the user what they meant first.

The confirmation step matters because a hesitant command can still have a clear intent. With `jev-1.14.0`, "Um, the transfer thing... yeah, go ahead I guess." got 0.99 for `approve_transfer`. That answer says which action the user wants, but not that the user has checked the transfer details.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **Why not `confidence`?** For a Choice question with a fixed number of options, `confidence` is calculated from the top probability, so a threshold on it adds nothing, and the probability is easier to read as risk. If it matters how the other options compare, check their probabilities too. Confidence is more useful for a Score, as in [Routing by confidence](/patterns/confidence-routing). Also take a look at [When to act on confidence](/confidence#when-to-act-on-confidence).


# Primitives (Questions)
Source: https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives

The System One question types, the typed answers they return, how to choose between them, and how to ask several at once.

TypeSafe's primitives are the small, typed building blocks you compose in code. They come in pairs: a question defines one judgment for a [System One model](/concepts/system-one) to make about a [state](/concepts/state), and its answer is the typed value that comes back. You compose the answers in your code to make decisions. Each question type returns a different shape of answer.

| Type | What it answers | Returns |
| - | - | - |
| [Choice](/primitives/choice) | Which of these options? | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Score](/primitives/score) | Which level? | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence` |
| [Noul](/primitives/noul) | Is this true? | `noul` (0 to 1) |
| [Box](/primitives/box) (Dreamer-ready) | Where is it in this image? | `box` (`top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`), `confidence` |

You can ask one question or send several together. Every question in a request sees the same state, is evaluated independently, and returns a typed answer under the ID you chose.

## Ask for one snap judgment per question

System One models are built for fast, focused judgments. Ask for a judgment a knowledgeable person makes in a second given the right context. "Does this message convey urgency?" is a good question. "Analyze this message and determine the best course of action" is not. That needs slow reasoning, and it is a signal to break the task into small questions and compose the answers in code.

If the judgment you want depends on several independent factors, ask about each factor separately and combine the answers with your own logic. Instead of "rate this startup pitch", ask about market size, technical feasibility, and differentiation, then weight them in code based on their relative importance. When priorities shift, change the value of weights rather than rewriting a prompt. [Ask multiple questions together](#ask-multiple-questions-together) shows how to do this.

## Define a question

Every question has an ID, a `type`, and `instructions`. Choice and Score questions also take `criteria`, which define the options for a Choice question or the levels for a Score. Noul questions accept `criteria` as an optional clarification of what yes and no mean.

* ID. The key you pick, such as `refund_requested`. It identifies the answer in the response.
* `type`. One of `choice`, `score`, `noul`, or `box` (Box is [Dreamer-ready](/primitives/box): a preview for prototypes, not yet for production).
* `instructions`. The question you are asking about the state. This is where your evaluation logic goes. Write it as a clear, specific question, or as a statement for the model to judge. A string is enough for most questions. It can also be an object or an array, which puts the question in one field and the data it refers to in others; see [Use structure in the questions](/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one#use-structure-in-the-questions).
* `criteria`. The possible answers: a map of options for a Choice question, an ordered list of levels for a Score, and an optional description of yes and no for a Noul. Each question type's page covers its shape.

This question asks whether a customer requested a refund:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Noul

questions = {
    "refund_requested": Noul(
        instructions="Does the customer request a refund?",
    ),
}
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Question IDs are for your code. They are not sent to the model. Write the complete question in `instructions`, even when the ID seems self-explanatory.

## Choose a question type

Pick the type that matches the shape of the answer you need.

* **Choice** fits when the answer is one of a known set of options with no order between them: routing a ticket to a department, classifying a document type, detecting a programming language. Give the full list of options. A Choice question always picks one, even when nothing fits, so when the list might not cover every input, add a [companion Noul](/patterns/companion-noul) to the same request that asks whether any option fits, and act on the Choice only when the Noul says yes. In our tests, this works better than an `other` or `none of the above` option, which competes with your real options for probability.

* **Score** fits when the answer falls on a spectrum and you can describe what each point on that spectrum means: bug severity, customer frustration, skill level. The levels are yours to define, and the model returns a position along them.

* **Noul** fits a clean yes/no question where the probability itself is the useful signal: does this message contain personally identifiable information, is the customer requesting a refund, does the resume mention distributed systems.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Use Noul for a yes/no judgment and Score to measure a position on a spectrum. "Is this candidate strong in Python?" needs a clear definition of "strong". A Noul value of 0.5 means the model gives yes and no equal probability. It does not mean the candidate has a medium skill level. An unclear definition makes that probability hard to interpret.
>
> If you want to measure skill level, use a Score with defined levels, such as no experience, some familiarity, daily use, and deep expertise. If you need a yes/no decision, define the condition clearly, such as "Does the resume state that the candidate has used Python at work?"

If two types both seem to fit, prefer the one whose answer your code can act on directly. A Choice between `refund`, `rebook`, and `information` maps straight onto three code paths. A Score of customer frustration maps onto a threshold. A Noul maps onto an `if`.

## What comes back

Answers are primitives too. Each question type returns a typed value that your code can compare, threshold, sort, pass into further logic, or put into the state of a follow-up request (see [When one question depends on another](#when-one-question-depends-on-another)).

| Type | Answer fields | How to read it |
| - | - | - |
| Choice | `choice`, `probabilities`, `confidence` | `choice` is the selected option. `probabilities` is the distribution across every option. `confidence` summarizes how peaked that distribution is. |
| Score | `score`, `legend`, `probabilities`, `confidence` | `score` is a position along your levels, and can fall between two of them. `legend` repeats the levels by number. `probabilities` is the distribution across levels. |
| Noul | `noul` | The probability that the answer is yes. Near 1 is a strong yes, near 0 a strong no, near 0.5 uncertain. Noul has no separate `confidence`. |
| Box (Dreamer-ready) | `box`, `confidence` | `box` holds the four edges, `top`, `bottom`, `left`, and `right`, each a fraction of the image's width or height from 0 to 1. A Box always returns a location, so pair it with a Noul question that asks whether the target is in the image at all. |

Two properties of these answers make them composable:

* **Every answer is constrained to the options you supplied.** The model returns a probability distribution over your options or levels, never a value outside them. Your code never has to recover a value from generated prose.
* **Every answer is independent.** One question's answer is not hidden context for another. You can add or remove questions without changing the others' results.

Some question types also return `confidence`; each type's page says whether its answers include it. [Confidence](/confidence) explains how to use it to decide when to act automatically and when to escalate to a person.

## Reference specific fields

The content being evaluated, the [state](/concepts/state), is often a JSON object with several parts: a conversation, a record, a policy. When a question is about one of those parts, name it in the `instructions` with a dot-and-index path to its key, including the backticks. The model then knows which part of the state to judge.

Take the support conversation from the State page:

```json theme={null}
{
  "ticket": {
    "subject": "Duplicate charge",
    "messages": [
      {"from": "customer", "text": "I was charged twice for order A-104. Please refund the duplicate."},
      {"from": "support", "text": "We are checking the charges."}
    ]
  },
  "order": {
    "id": "A-104",
    "charges": [
      {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"},
      {"amount_usd": 49, "status": "captured"}
    ]
  },
  "refund_policy": "Duplicate charges are eligible for a refund."
}
```

These two questions point at the customer's message, the policy, and the charges by path:

```python theme={null}
questions = {
    "refund_requested": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Does `ticket.messages[0].text` request a refund?",
    },
    "policy_supports_refund": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": (
            "Does `refund_policy` support the refund requested "
            "in `ticket.messages[0].text`, given `order.charges`?"
        ),
    },
}
```

Explicit paths make it clear which parts of a structured state should inform each judgment. See [State](/concepts/state) for how to structure the input.

## Ask multiple questions together

Send every question that uses the same state in one request. You can mix question types freely. System One models evaluate every question in a request in parallel. Adding questions barely changes the response time and costs only the tokens for the extra questions, which are cheap. Asking a question you might not need is close to free.

This request classifies a customer message, checks for urgency, and scores frustration all at once:

Try it in the Playground →

Our [client SDKs](/sdk) provide typed questions and answers. In Python, pass a `questions` dictionary of `Choice`, `Noul`, and `Score` objects to `client.system_one(...)`. This request sends a ticket and a refund policy once and gets a typed answer for each question:

```python theme={null}
from typesafe_sdk import Choice, Noul, Score, TypeSafeClient

state = {
    "ticket_message": "My flight was cancelled. Can I get a refund?",
    "refund_policy": "Cancelled flights are eligible for a full refund.",
}

with TypeSafeClient() as client:
    response = client.system_one(
        state=state,
        questions={
            "refund_requested": Noul(
                instructions="Does `ticket_message` request a refund?",
            ),
            "request_type": Choice(
                instructions="What is the main request in `ticket_message`?",
                criteria={
                    "refund": "The customer wants money returned.",
                    "rebooking": "The customer wants a replacement flight.",
                    "information": "The customer is asking for information only.",
                },
            ),
            "frustration": Score(
                instructions="How frustrated does the customer appear in `ticket_message`?",
                criteria=[
                    "Calm and neutral.",
                    "Concerned but civil.",
                    "Very angry or using strong language.",
                ],
            ),
        },
    )

print(response.answers["refund_requested"].noul)
print(response.answers["request_type"].choice)
print(response.answers["frustration"].score)
```

See [client SDKs](/sdk) for installation and usage in your language.

### Ask speculative questions

Ask every question your code might need, including ones whose answer only matters for some inputs, and let the code decide which answers to use. If a ticket turns out not to be a bug report, ignore the severity answer. We call this the [Speculative fan-out](/patterns/fan-out) pattern. The [Parallel questions cookbook](/cookbooks/parallel_questions) shows how batching 13 questions into one call is 11.5x cheaper and 9.6x faster than 13 separate calls, with no change in the answers.

> [!TIP]
>
> Coding agents fall into the one question per request habit more than people do. The [TypeSafe agent skill](/agent-skill#installation) tells your agent to put many questions in each request, including ones that only matter for some inputs.

### How many questions you can ask

There is no limit on the number of questions in a request. What limits a request is its size: it has to fit the model's [per-request context and per-question context](/models#context-length).

Questions are often short compared with the `state`, in which case the `state` takes up most of both. If your questions don't all fit in one request, one option is to spread them across several requests with the same `state`.

### Split a complex judgment into several questions

A judgment that depends on several things is best split into one question per thing. Combine the answers in your code, giving each a weight for its relative importance. The weights are yours. When the combined result doesn't match what your team would decide, change them in code and run again. Adding questions barely changes the response time because they run in parallel within one request. The split costs a few extra question tokens.

For example, ticket priority might be built from three Score questions: how severe the bug is, how frustrated the customer is, and how much the report gives an engineer to work with. The Score page walks through this request and the code that normalizes and weights the answers in [Splitting a complex judgment into several Scores](/primitives/score#splitting-a-complex-judgment-into-several-score-questions). This technique is called the [Composite scoring](/patterns/composite-scoring) pattern.

### When one question depends on another

Questions in the same request are independent: one answer does not become context for another question. If a later judgment depends on an earlier answer, make a second request in code. The dependency is real only when your code cannot build the second request until it has the first answer: it needs the answer to fetch more data for the state, to decide what the state is made of, or to pick the next question's options. Otherwise, ask the questions together and combine their answers in code.

Two requests are the exception, not the rule. If the second request's questions could have been asked against the original state, ask them in the first request and let the code ignore the ones it doesn't need. Three cookbooks make a second request for a real reason. [Skill suggestion](/cookbooks/skill_suggestion) ranks 182 skills in one request, then fetches the full text of the top three and judges them again against that better evidence. [Structure recovery](/cookbooks/autoformat) asks whether each line break split a sentence, merges lines into blocks from those answers, then classifies the blocks, which did not exist until the first request had answered. [Hierarchical classification](/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification) uses each Choice answer to decide which options the next request offers.

See [How to build with TypeSafe](/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one) for guidance on breaking a workflow into focused judgments.

## Next steps

> [card] [Choice](/primitives/choice)
>
> Pick one option from a fixed list.

> [card] [Score](/primitives/score)
>
> Rate the state along ordered levels.

> [card] [Noul](/primitives/noul)
>
